#7926. Jennifer Garner reveals how Once Upon a Farm became a $724 million company without sacrificing its values at Motherly’s State of Motherhood event

Home / Health & Wellness / Women's Health

Motherly hosted some of the country’s most influential women leaders for a State of Motherhood event that took a deep look at what the last decade reveals about moms, and what we need going forward.

By Audrey Goodson Kingo Updated Nov. 19, 2026

Moms may be burned out and lonely right now – but we don’t have to accept it.

That was the theme of Motherly’s State of Motherhood event on Monday, which brought together some of the most powerful women in business, media and advocacy to diagnose how moms have fared during the last tumultuous decade, and detail what we need going forward.

The conversation was driven by an in-depth analysis of Motherly’s own research. Every year since 2018, we’ve polled thousands of moms (more than 60,000 in fact!) for our annual State of Motherhood survey. And every year, moms have told us they’re scaling back at work and having fewer children than they’d prefer, but they’re still feeling isolated and overwhelmed. In 2025, 70% of moms said motherhood is lonelier than expected and in 2026, 42% felt more burned out than in the previous year.

“The truth is that our expectations of what it means to be a good mom changed faster than the systems built around to support her, and Gen Z moms are running into that gap even earlier,” said Motherly’s CEO Sharon Yi in her opening remarks. “But none of us should have to sacrifice our sanity, our careers, our identities to have children, and no mother should have to carry it alone.”

Leaders from organizations at the Clinton Foundation, the Andrew Carnegie Foundation, the ACLU, and the Vote Mama Foundation, joined together with executives at JP Morgan, Pfizer, Coterie, IKEA, and Paramount, to hear from women who are working tirelessly to create a world where moms feel supported, connected, and respected.

That included actress Jennifer Garner, who talked about her work as an ambassador for Save the Children and as co-founder of organic children’s nutrition company Once Upon a Farm.

Garner kicked off the event in a fireside chat that touched on everything from finding community as a mom to the importance of advocating for children and families.

“Every kid deserves healthy, real food, an education, and parents who have a roof over their heads, food in their bellies, and time and space and energy and support to love their kids,” she said. Traveling around the country for her work with Save the Children, she described seeing families stretch food-bank, WIC, and SNAP resources to feed their children.

That’s why Once Upon a Farm worked hard to become the first WIC-certified company offering organic refrigerated baby food, she said. The company is now WIC-certified in 22 states. For Garner, it’s about dignity and choice: families using public benefits should be able to access high-quality food.

It’s all baked in, pun intended, to the company’s social mission to “drive systemic change in childhood nutrition for a happier, healthier, more equitable world,” Garner says. In 2021, the company transitioned its corporate structure from an LLC to a Public Benefit Corporation (PBC), which legally requires it to balance profitability with its social and environmental impact. It’s a challenging path for a business to pursue, which is why there are fewer than 20 publicly-traded PBCs, and Once Upon a Farm is the only one focused on kids. Towards those goals, Garner said, the company has donated a million meals to kids in rural America, and it pays a premium for produce “so that the people who are growing and picking our food are recruited ethically, and have a say in their safety and what their workday looks like.”

When it comes to balancing the demands of her multi-hyphenite life with motherhood, Garner didn’t hold back. On her non-negotiables, she joked, “I work out every day… unless I don’t. I read every night until I fall asleep… one page or none. I go to church… when I can. My kids come first… except for weeks where it’s crazy and I tell them they come first from afar.”

Finding the right balance changes day by day, Garner said. She assesses who needs her most in a given moment, including herself. “You get to choose moment to moment what you do and what your family needs,” she said to the moms in the room.

She also encouraged moms to come together to help defeat the loneliness that Motherly’s data revealed. “We’re literally meant to be in community,” she described. “When my second was born, I joined a baby group for second-time moms, and that is the most active group chat on my phone to this day.”

Plus, she added, small groups of committed moms have the power to make real change.

“We all love our babies the same. And when you realize that, that every mother in the world loves their baby the way you love yours, which seems impossible, but it is true, that also connects you to every other mother,” she said. “And then you feel like, how can I help every other mother who doesn’t have the advantages I have?”

Next up was a panel about the state of motherhood in 2026, breaking down Motherly’s data showing that moms are increasingly burned out, and figuring out fixes to help. Featuring some of the most influential women working to make the United States a better place for families, the panelists pointed out that burnout is a structural problem — not an individual failure — and that collective action can turn broad public support for family policies into change.

“I think motherhood in America is impossible by design,” said Reshma Saujani, the founder and CEO of Moms First, a national non-profit organization working to advance paid leave and affordable childcare for working families. “Why does the school day end at 2:30 and the workday end at six? Why do we pay more for our childcare than our mortgage? Why do one out of four women go back to work two weeks after having a baby?”

Lauren Smith Brody, the founder of The Fifth Trimester and co-founder of Chamber of Mothers, said she’s optimistic that federal lawmakers will soon advance legislation to help moms across the country, including paid family leave, affordable childcare for all, and measures to improve maternal health outcomes. “I feel a lot of hope as we walk into these offices on Capitol Hill and we make a lot of behind the scenes connections between Democratic offices and Republican offices, because guess what? They actually do want many of the same things,” she said. “Moms are top of the list. They know that our voting power is unmatched. They know that they need us. They know that we voted them in and can vote them out.”

“I am telling you standing right here, [affordable] childcare and paid leave will get passed in 2029 within the first hundred days,” Saujani said. “I don’t care who is elected president because we are getting this done.”

It’s all about moms coming together to hold leaders accountable, said Ailen Arreaza, the executive director of the national nonprofit parents organization ParentsTogether. “Moms often feel it’s our sole responsibility to protect our kids, and feel shame when we think we’ve failed — especially when it comes to technology,” she said. “One of the best ways that we can hold companies accountable is by sharing our stories. We do a lot of work with parents who have lost children to big tech, and their stories are so powerful,” she said. “That also helps with the shame. When we talk to each other about what we are struggling with, what we are facing, that shame evaporates.”

Michelle Jawando, the CEO of Omidyar Network, a philanthropy organization working to foster responsible technology and AI development, said she’s encouraged by the fact that the mistakes of the “move-fast-and-break-things” era in Silicon Valley are providing a roadmap for more responsible tech development going forward. “I believe that everything that happened in that proceeding era gives us an opportunity to get AI right,” she said, pointing to California, which recently passed the strongest AI companion chatbot legislation in the country.

The morning’s final panel, moderated by the host of Motherly’s new podcast, Daniela Gysler-Wood, provided practical ways mothers can protect their physical and mental well-being.

Dr. Bayo Curry-Winchell, a board certified family medicine physician and the author of the upcoming book How to Talk to Your Doctor, encouraged moms to keep seeking answers if they’re feeling unwell. Her advice? If a clinician says you are fine but you do not feel fine, say, “I understand that you think I’m fine, but I’m not. What are the next steps?”

She also suggested asking, “What three to five possibilities are on your working list?” This helps you understand the range of possibilities if your doctor is focused on just one diagnosis.

When it comes to getting enough rest, celebrate the small wins, said Megan Holm, the women’s sleep research lead at sleep technology company Eight Sleep. “Sleep when you can, and you don’t need to check off everything on your to-do list in order to put your head on the pillow. You can take a 30-minute nap,” she said.

“I think we’ve all just accepted that exhaustion is part of motherhood, and I don’t think that’s where we should be,” said Victoria Thain Gioia, the co-founder and CEO of Perelel, an OB/GYN-founded and doctor-formulated vitamin and supplement brand. “To get through the day and stay sane, and to take care of small children, and do your job, you need to be nutritionally sufficient, not depleted. So while it can sometimes be overhyped, the conversation about protein, collagen, lactoferrin and nutrients that can actually support your energy [is important]. We really need to focus on care for mom beyond just pregnancy and postpartum.”

When it comes to protecting our mental well-being, the panelists encouraged moms to let go of guilt and connect with other parents. “Check in on your friends, nurture your friendships, don’t ask everything of your partner or your spouse, and ask for help,” said Elise Hu, the host of TED Talks Daily, a flagship podcast from TED Conferences. “Asking for help doesn’t just benefit you, the person who needs the help, it also benefits the helper because think about all the times that you have been asked for advice or counsel. That’s such a tribute to you, right? Because somebody is saying to you, ‘I trust you and I trust your advice and I trust your counsel.’ It nurtures the connection on both ends, not only for the helpee, but also the helper.”

The moms in the room didn’t just leave with actionable advice and encouragement – although there was plenty on tap – they also took home a Happ Paige Mini full of goodies, including Once Upon a Farm snacks, Perelel Collagen+ Defense Supplements, Shiseido Sun Protector Clear Stick Sunscreen, Then I Met You Cleansing Balm, Ursa Major Golden Hour Recovery Cream, Merit Shade Slick, and the new Bentgo Lift Chug Lid water bottle.

Guests also got a chance to try out a mini version of Eight Sleep’s pod, an intelligent mattress cover that uses built-in biometric sensors to track your sleep and automatically adjust its temperature. “In May, we released pregnancy mode, which is automatic temperature support to support women as they go through pregnancy and up to 24 weeks postpartum,” said Holm, Eight Sleep’s women’s research lead, during the second panel. “As you grow a child, the environment around you feels really hot and uncomfortable. So we automatically make sure that when you can rest, and even if it’s not for eight hours every night, you’re comfortable.”

And bestselling author Loryn Brantz greeted guests as they walked into the room, signing free copies of her new release, I Am a Spicy Nugget, as well as copies of her New York Times bestseller, Poems of Parenting. Some lucky guests also received a signed print.

Motherly’s CEO Sharon Yi closed out the day with a call to action for all of the “incredible, powerful, influential” women in the room: “From all these conversations, I heard over and over that we need community, and that community is power, big or small,” she began. “We need advocates, people who fight relentlessly for the care, the policies and the respect that moms deserve. And we need storytellers, people who show the real picture of this journey at every stage without judgment.”

That’s where Motherly can play a powerful role going forward, she noted.

“Motherly is growing from a trusted resource into an active community online and off,” she explained. “What does that mean in practice? It means we’re showing up in her group chat. We’re in her feed with a slate of new vertical video shows that I’m really excited about. We’re in her earbuds with a new podcast. And we’re popping up in her neighborhood with our new hyper local event series, coming to a neighborhood near you so that moms can find the people where they are.”

#7925. My Husband Wants To Bring His Girlfriend To Thanksgiving. I’m Not Sure I’m Ready.

Just because we have an open relationship doesn’t mean I’m ready for such a big step.

Welcome to Ask A MWLTF (Yes, that’s Mother Who Likes to F*ck.), a monthly anonymous advice column from Scary Mommy. Here we’ll dissect all your burning questions about motherhood, sex, romance, intimacy, and friendship with the help of our columnist, Penelope, a writer and mental health practitioner in training. She’ll dish out her most sound advice for parents on the delicate dance of raising kids without sacrificing other important relationships. Email her at askpenelope@scarymommy.com.

My husband and I have been open for about two years. It was something we discussed carefully, and, for the most part, it has worked for us. We have rules, we communicate, and I’ve met a couple of the women he’s dated. I’m not interested in knowing every detail, but I also don’t feel threatened by the fact that he has relationships outside our marriage.

Now he’s been seeing someone for about six months, and he wants to bring her to Thanksgiving at my parents’ house.

We have two kids, and Thanksgiving is a big family holiday for us. My parents, siblings, nieces and nephews will all be there. My husband says he wants to stop treating this relationship like something that has to be kept separate from the rest of his life. He says he’s serious about her and thinks including her would make things feel more natural and less secretive.

I understand that. But I also feel strangely territorial. Thanksgiving is one of the few days of the year when I get to be with my whole family, and I don’t particularly want to spend it navigating my husband’s girlfriend. I’m worried about what my parents will think, what the kids will make of it, and whether I’ll spend the entire day feeling like I’m auditioning for the role of Cool, Secure Wife.

I don’t want to be controlling or make him feel ashamed of a relationship that I’ve agreed he can have. But I also don’t want to be pushed into a level of openness I haven’t agreed to. Am I being unreasonable?

It's easy for pressure to arise in a consensually non-monogamous relationship, and it often wears the very respectable outfit of personal growth. You have agreed to be open-minded, so shouldn’t you be open? You have agreed that your husband can love or desire other people, so shouldn’t you be comfortable meeting them? And if you’re not comfortable, does that mean you’re secretly jealous, insecure, or not as evolved as you thought you were?

No. It means you are a person with boundaries, and boundaries do not disappear just because you have made an unconventional relationship choice.

One of the more persistent misunderstandings about non-monogamy is that consent to one arrangement somehow implies consent to all the arrangements that might follow from it. But agreeing that your husband can date other people is not the same as agreeing that those people will become part of your family life. Being comfortable with his girlfriend existing is not the same as wanting her seated next to your Aunt Carol while everyone argues about the turkey.

These are different levels of intimacy. They involve different audiences, different risks, and different emotional demands. You can be genuinely supportive of your husband’s relationship and still want to keep Thanksgiving to the people who have traditionally been part of Thanksgiving.

In fact, I wonder if what you’re reacting to is not simply the presence of another woman, but the feeling that a boundary you thought was understood is being moved. Until now, your husband’s outside relationships have occupied a particular space in your marriage. They may be meaningful, even serious, but they have not been woven into the rituals that organize your family life. Bringing his girlfriend to Thanksgiving would change that. It would make the relationship visible to your parents and children, and it would ask you to participate in presenting it as part of the family.

That is a significant request. It deserves more than a casual, “Wouldn’t it be nice if she came?”

Your husband may have a legitimate desire to stop compartmentalizing. He may feel that keeping his girlfriend separate from his family life makes her seem less important, or that the secrecy itself is beginning to feel uncomfortable. Those feelings are worth taking seriously. But his desire for integration does not automatically create an obligation for you to provide it, particularly on a holiday that belongs to your family history as much as it belongs to your marriage.

And let’s talk about the children. There is nothing inherently harmful about children knowing that a parent has a romantic relationship with someone other than their spouse. But introducing a partner into family life is not a neutral logistical decision. It raises questions about what the children understand, what they have been told, what they might repeat to relatives, and whether the adults have a shared explanation. If your husband wants his girlfriend to be part of family gatherings, the two of you need to agree on what that means before you put a new person in the middle of a holiday and hope everyone figures it out over pie.

I would also encourage you to resist the temptation to make this a referendum on how good you are at non-monogamy. You do not have to prove your security by accepting every proposed next step. Sometimes the most honest thing you can say is, “I’m okay with your relationship, but I’m not ready for it to occupy this particular space in my life.”

That is not a punishment. It is information.

You might tell your husband something like: “I understand why you want the people in your life to know one another, and I’m not asking you to hide or minimize this relationship. But Thanksgiving with my family feels like too big a first step. I need us to talk about what integrating our relationships into family life would look like, and I don’t want to make that decision under pressure or on a holiday.”

Then get specific. Does he want you to meet her in a lower-stakes setting first? Does he imagine that she will attend future family events? Does he want the children to know about the relationship? What does she want? Is she comfortable being introduced to your parents as your husband’s girlfriend? And what happens if you discover that you like her, but still don’t want to share Thanksgiving with her? Or if you don’t like her? Or if your husband expects you to be warm and welcoming in a way that feels emotionally dishonest?

These are not small details. They are the actual relationship you’re negotiating.

There is another possibility worth considering: Your husband may be asking for something that sounds like inclusion but is, at least in part, a request for reassurance. Perhaps he wants to know that you accept his girlfriend, that he doesn’t have to split his life into separate compartments, that his happiness won’t always be experienced as a threat to your marriage. If so, you can offer reassurance without agreeing to this particular plan. You can say, “I don’t want you to feel ashamed of this relationship. I just don’t want to make Thanksgiving the place where we figure out how to live with it.”

And if he insists that your reluctance means you aren’t truly comfortable with non-monogamy, I would push back. A relationship agreement is not a blank check. It is an ongoing negotiation, and the terms can become more complicated as people’s feelings and circumstances change. You are allowed to discover that something you thought you could handle feels different when it moves from the abstract to the dining room.

So perhaps the question isn’t whether his girlfriend gets to come to Thanksgiving this year. It’s whether the two of you can talk about the future of your family life without either of you treating the other’s feelings as evidence of a moral failing. He should be able to tell you that he wants more integration. You should be able to tell him that you’re not ready. Neither of you gets to turn your preference into the only enlightened position.

And for what it’s worth, Thanksgiving is already a holiday with enough emotional labor, complicated family dynamics, and people pretending to enjoy casseroles they hate. You are not obligated to add a major relationship milestone to the menu.

You can take this one holiday at a time. The turkey will survive.

Your garden beds may be looking tired, but there's no need for back-breaking work. Just four simple layers can help replenish them in time for spring planting.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Just because you like gardening doesn’t mean that you enjoy every landscape task. Some of us gardeners love planting flowers but don’t enjoy raking leaves. Others like tucking mulch around their shrubs but won’t pull weeds. But digging up the garden dirt and turning it over is not high on anyone’s list of favorite tasks.

So just say no to digging in the fall and say yes to lasagna gardening. It’s a clever, no-dig technique that works best in fall. Leave the shovel in the garage and instead, stack layers of cardboard, fallen leaves, and other organic materials over the garden soil, letting them break down naturally over winter. The result is fertile planting beds for spring.

Ready to get “cooking”? Here, I will walk you through the four-layer lasagna garden recipe.

Of course you love your garden, but wouldn’t it be nice if the garden could do most of the work of preparing the beds for spring planting? Lasagna gardening, aka no-dig or no-till gardening, allows your garden to do most of the work of decomposition and replenishment. The technique is really cold composting in place.

This low-effort process works like home composting: alternate layers of green and brown materials, then let them break down into the soil. Cut grass and kitchen scraps are green materials; cardboard and dried leaves are brown materials. Your “lasagna” is a compost heap waiting to happen.

You can also think of lasagna gardening as mimicking the forest floor. It works the same way soil is built up in a woodland. First, leaves pile up and decompose on the forest floor. Along come microbes and worms that transform that debris into rich soil. Lasagna gardening follows the same pattern, making your garden bed into a soil ecosystem.

When you make a lasagna for dinner, you just layer up the pasta, the ragù, the sauce, and grated cheese, then pop it in the oven. Without any additional work on your part, a luscious dinner will be ready when it is time to eat.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

A winter lasagna garden uses the same system. You stack up four layers, then leave it to decompose. Without any additional work on your part, your garden will have rich, fertile soil for spring. Here are the four key layers.

Think of cardboard as the weed barrier. First, weed-whack or mow the area to cut down any weeds or grass. A cordless string trimmer, like this Worx model, makes things easier.

Then, lay sheets of flattened cardboard right over the soil in your garden, using overlapping layers to cover the entire area. Heavy, corrugated cardboard works best to keep grass and weeds out while still welcoming earthworms. After that is done, douse all of the cardboard with lukewarm water.

This is the carbon layer, supporting soil microbes and providing structural aeration. I like using dry autumn leaves (what else are you going to do with them?), but a thick layer of any type of brown material will work, giving your garden soil a carbon-rich environment. Alternatives include straw, peat moss, sawdust, wood chips, or shredded newspaper.

If you don't have enough waste materials to hand, a bag of garden straw mulch, like this HealthiStraw GardenStraw from Walmart, is an easy way to bulk up this layer.

Here’s the “compost” element of the lasagna. Your green materials will be in charge of making the garden soil a nitrogen-rich environment that heats up and fuels the decay process. Together with the brown material, they make the garden one giant compost pile. You can use kitchen waste, but also toss in some grass clippings, coffee grounds, or even manure.

If you can't source enough green material for free, then pick up a bag of composted cow manure, such as Black Kow, available at Home Depot.

You aren’t limited to one layer of brown material and one layer of green. Keep right on stacking alternating layers, using about twice as much brown as green. Two, three, or even four alternating layers of organic material can speed things up for your garden bed.

Flattened cardboard lays the foundation for the lasagna; compost or topsoil serves as a top cap. For a ready-made option, try Back to the Roots Organic Compost from Home Depot. This is especially important if you are planning on planting immediately. This rich layer is at the top of the pile so that your seeds will have what it takes to establish strong roots in short order.

A lasagna garden is an attractive option if low-maintenance is a priority. Once you create your lasagna, wonderful things begin to happen and keep on happening all winter. The green and brown layered materials function as a compost pile, and the constant interplay between them heats up, then breaks down the entire pile, enriching the soil.

The bottom layer of cardboard in the garden lasagna blocks weeds from invading the new, appealing soil. What had been a used-up garden transforms into a sanctuary for your plants, with loose, fertile soil. This makes the next growing season easy and exciting.

If you “build” a lasagna garden in the late autumn or early winter, the magic starts right away. The four layers do their job: the cardboard prevents weed growth, the brown and green layers do their compost dance and decompose into the soil, and the top layer is ready to welcome seeds.

This lasagna garden should be fully decomposed and ready to plant by the following April or May. Autumn rain and winter moisture keep the layers moist. The organic layers require at least several months to break down.

If you put in a lasagna garden in spring or summer, you do so with the thought of immediate planting. Just dig small pockets into the top layer of the bed.

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

#7921. Lights Out, Zoomies On: Why Dogs Go Wild at Bedtime

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

While nighttime zoomies are a well-recognized phenomenon in the feline world, it turns out dogs can also get a little over-excited at the prospect of bedtime. Just as the house is settling down for the night, a dog may start bouncing around, digging into the blankets, or demanding attention.

It also turns out that there isn't a single explanation for this evening burst of energy; there are several. The bed itself can be exciting, particularly because it smells like a favorite person and offers a chance for interaction. In other cases, a dog may simply have energy left to burn. Understanding the possible reasons can help explain why bedtime sometimes turns into playtime.

Dogs spend much of their time looking up at people from the floor. Climbing onto a bed changes that perspective, bringing a dog much closer to its owner's face and making interaction easier.

That alone can be enough to spark a playful mood. A dog may drop into a play bow, bark for attention, or bounce around in an attempt to encourage its person to join in.

Being face to face can make play feel more inviting, particularly for dogs that enjoy close interaction with their owners. What looks like a sudden burst of energy may simply be a dog making the most of the opportunity to engage on a different level.

A bed carries the scent of the person who sleeps in it, making it an especially interesting place for a dog to explore. Dogs rely heavily on their noses to understand their surroundings, and familiar smells can be particularly appealing.

For a dog that enjoys spending time with its owner, the bed may be one of the most comforting and interesting places in the home. Rolling around on the sheets or sniffing the blankets lets a dog investigate those familiar scents while enjoying a spot associated with its favorite person.

That combination of comfort, familiarity, and excitement can help explain why some dogs become especially playful once they climb onto the mattress.

For dogs that love burrowing, a bed covered in sheets and blankets can feel like an invitation to play. Digging, wriggling underneath the covers, and pushing through folds of fabric can all become part of the fun.

Some breeds are particularly inclined toward this kind of behavior. Dachshunds, for example, were bred to pursue animals such as badgers and weasels into their burrows. Their instinct to dig and tunnel can make a pile of blankets especially appealing. Meanwhile, Chihuahuas seem to be particularly fond of burrowing into the warmth and security of their humanâs bed.

A dog that discovers the pleasure of diving between the sheets may quickly turn it into a regular bedtime activity.

Dogs are often quick to learn which behaviors get a reaction from their owners. Climbing onto the bed puts them right where they're difficult to ignore, particularly if they start bouncing around or nudging someone for attention.

Bedtime can also signal that the day is winding down and an opportunity for cuddling is approaching. A dog that enjoys being close to its owner may become excited at the prospect of spending that time together.

If playful behavior consistently earns attention, a dog may be encouraged to repeat it. What begins as a burst of excitement can become a familiar part of the nightly routine. Even if this nightly ritual isnât one you welcome, waving arms and raised voices often count as a positive interaction for a dog, so if youâre trying to get your dog off the bed, be careful your methods align with your message.

Sometimes, a dog becomes especially energetic at bedtime simply because theyâre not ready to settle down. If it hasn't had enough exercise or stimulation during the day, the bed may become an outlet for that leftover energy.

A dog that is still eager to run, jump, and play may need more activity before the household turns in for the night. An evening walk or a game of tug-of-war can help provide an opportunity to burn off some energy before bedtime.

A dog that's had enough exercise and stimulation is more likely to be ready to relax, rather than treating the mattress as a playground.

Many owners enjoy sleeping alongside their dogs, while others prefer to keep their beds pet-free. Sharing a bed can feel cozy and comforting, and having a dog nearby may also be soothing for people who experience anxiety or other mental health challenges.

There are practical considerations, too. Dogs can carry dirt, bacteria, and parasites into the bed, and some owners would rather not have fur on their sheets or pillows.

Ultimately, whether a dog is allowed to sleep on the bed comes down to what works for the household. If itâs not a problem, then itâs not a problem. There's no single right choice, and a dog can still enjoy plenty of affection and companionship without sharing the mattress.

If you do want your bed to be a dog-free zone, the simplest solution is to keep the bedroom door closed. But if youâre simply looking for a way to get them off the bed without it turning into a party, a calm and quiet approach is best. A single command or using a slip-lead to silently guide them off the bed will be far more effective than shouting and pointing.

A dog getting frisky on the bed is often responding to a combination of familiar scents, opportunities for attention, and the chance to play somewhere comfortable. Blankets can add to the appeal, especially for dogs that enjoy burrowing.

If the behavior seems excessive, however, it may be worth looking at how much exercise and stimulation the dog gets during the day. Adding a walk or play session before bed can help make the transition to sleep easier.

For many dogs, the bed is simply an exciting place to be close to their favorite person. With a little preparation, bedtime can still end in a peaceful night's sleep rather than an impromptu wrestling match.

#7920. School meals decoded: What’s really on the lunch tray

The menu in your child’s cafeteria isn’t set by chance. It’s the result of a multi-year federal process, and you can weigh in on how it changes.

By Lauren Ramakrishna Updated Nov. 23, 2026

This article is sponsored by Center for Science in the Public Interest (CSPI). Thank you for supporting the brands that support Motherly and mamas.

In my son’s school district, entering middle school is a rite of passage. Sixth graders go to a new building, get their own locker, and experience freedoms they weren’t allowed in elementary school.

When my son came home from his first day of middle school, I couldn’t wait to talk about it. “What was the best part of your day?” I eagerly asked. “The food,” he replied.

I wasn’t surprised. Meals are a big deal for a growing boy. But it did make me wonder, what exactly will he eat for lunch every day?

Long gone are the days when I would pack my son a homemade lunch with a loving note tucked inside. In middle school, he wanted to walk into the cafeteria, review the day’s menu options, stand in line, and buy his lunch. I agreed to the plan because I wanted to support his thirst for independence. But I also hoped I hadn’t unwittingly given him permission to start a junk-food-only diet.

Luckily, there are guidelines schools are required to follow when it comes to serving our kids meals. Those rules aim to make lunchtime enjoyable and healthy for the 30 million students who eat school lunch every day in the United States through the National School Lunch Program (NSLP). Unsurprisingly, they’re a constant work in progress.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) sets federal requirements for school meals served through the NSLP and the School Breakfast Program. The rules attempt to align school food offerings with nutrition standards outlined in the Dietary Guidelines for Americans (DGA), the official dietary guidance published by the USDA and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) every five years. When the DGA gets an update, school nutrition standard changes will follow, as required by law.

Schools are currently implementing changes developed following the release of the 2020-2025 DGA. In April 2024, the Food and Nutrition Administration (FNA, formerly Food and Nutrition Service) , a government agency responsible for administering domestic nutrition programs, like the NSLP, issued a rule requiring schools to make changes to foods served at school, including:

These updates join a comprehensive list of nutrition standards for school breakfasts and lunches that outline weekly serving requirements for fruits, vegetables, grains, meats and meat alternatives, and milk, as well as calorie minimums and maximums, and limits on saturated fat.

The USDA and HHS released the 2025-2030 DGA on January 7, 2026, triggering the next wave of school nutrition reviews in preparation for new recommendations and requirements. The USDA will compare the new DGA guidelines against existing school nutrition requirements, then draft a proposed rule on which schools, state agencies, advocates, industry experts, and consumer advocacy groups, like Center for the Science in the Public Interest, can provide feedback. The USDA will read and respond to comments, sometimes changing planned provisions in response to the feedback received, then publish its final rule.

At face value, this may seem like a good thing.

The USDA and HHS appoints a Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee (DGAC) every five years to serve as an independent, expert panel of scientists and researchers in nutrition, health and medicine. The committee spends years reviewing current nutrition science to write a scientific report that’s typically used as a foundational resource for new dietary guidelines. DGAs have historically followed the vast majority of the DGAC’s recommendations. But, as CSPI notes, USDA and HHS rejected more than half of the DGAC’s expert recommendations. Instead, the agencies, according to CSPI,  “hand-picked authors whose work aligned with beef, dairy, and protein supplement industry interests and the administration’s preconceived policy goals.”

This group of hand-picked authors created a new “Scientific Foundation for Dietary Guidelines for Americans,” which includes contradictory advice, recommending folks stick to prior, science-based saturated fat limits, while suggesting high-fat foods like whole milk and beef tallow are part of a healthy diet.

CSPI has raised other concerns about the 2025-2030 DGA, arguing that it gives harmful guidance to emphasize animal protein; advises people to consume double or more of the scientifically-backed recommendation for daily protein; reduces clarity around how people can eat a balanced diet within vegetable and protein categories; and adopts an inverted food pyramid that doesn’t accurately visually represent the dietary recommendations found within the text of the guidelines.

As in cycles past, schools expect the USDA to use the most recent DGA as a guide to propose changes to school nutrition standards. It’s unclear exactly what changes will be put forth, but there will likely be a mix of nutrition wins and losses. It’s possible the new standards will reflect evidence-based nutrition guidance like increasing whole grains, protein, and whole fruit, and cutting back on added sugars, sodium, and refined grains in school meals.

However, it’s also likely the new proposed standards may stray from evidence-based guidance by calling for decreased vegetable variety and overall fiber intake due to a deprioritization of plant-based proteins and an overemphasis on high-fat foods like whole milk and beef (rather than a variety of protein sources).  For example, students could see more protein, like eggs and yogurt, at breakfast but miss out on a rainbow of vegetables and inclusive protein options like beans and tofu at lunch. Zooming out, meals lower in added sugars could be prioritized, while progress made on reducing saturated fat and sodium in school meals will be lost.

The best way to inform what your kids get on their breakfast and lunch trays at school is to make your voice heard. After proposing changes to nutrition standards, the government will open a public comment period where you can share your opinions about what should be included or excluded from school meals. When the proposed rule finally comes out, CSPI will make it easy to share your opinion through model comments and templates that will allow parents to comment directly on the proposed rule. Stay tuned for next steps by signing up for CSPI advocacy emails.

The regulatory red tape may seem overwhelming. That’s why non-profits like CSPI give parents tools to learn about school nutrition standards and enact change. To learn more about school nutrition standards, visit CSPI’s Healthier School Food advocacy page. If you’re ready to advocate for healthier school meals, check out CPSI’s Take Action page to get involved.

#7919. Best Splurge Gifts 2026: 18 Luxury Gifts Worth The Money

Yes, they’re splurges. No, we don’t regret a single one.

We all enter the holiday season with the best intentions: to get gifts that will bring our loved ones joy, ideally without devastating our bank accounts. But the reality is there’s almost always at least one gift that you break your own budget rule for, and it’s usually the thing you keep circling around. You open the tab, you close the tab, you try to convince yourself you don’t actually need said item, you text your sister, “Would it be insane to buy this?!”

And, yes, sometimes it is insane. In this economy? A quick trip to the grocery store can feel like a splurge. But maybe that’s all the more reason to give yourself permission to make an exception or two this holiday season. We could all use a little extra joy right now. Even better if it’s something that makes your life easier or more enjoyable somehow — the kind of gift that gets used every single day or makes an annoying part of your routine more bearable.

Those are the gifts on this list. Our editors picked the pricier stuff that has actually earned its spot in our homes. A light mask that will have people asking if you just got a facial. A giant fort that’ll take over your living room but be the source of so much laughter. Is any of it cheap? Nope. Is it all worth it? Well, we’d stake our holiday budgets on it. (Again.)

Now that it's getting cooler out -- and my skin has fully made the transition -- I start entertaining the idea of taking baths. Cause when you get right down to it, baths are pretty luxurious, especially if you're a busy mom. I LOVE the scent of this product. It's like taking an Italian vacation in your very own tub. All of Seed to Skin's products are free of parabens, toxins and fillers, to name a few. So go ahead and treat yourself to a little luxury -- you'll thank yourself later. — Kate Auletta, Editor-in-Chief

I got serious about dutifully using retinol this year, and I also wanted to see if the hype around red light masks was warranted. Between the two, I definitely get a ton of compliments about my skin now. The Luyors mask has been fantastic; I love that it treats my neck and chest as well as my face. It holds a charge forever, and has so many different light modes depending on what your skin concerns are. This is a fantastic splurge-worthy gift for yourself or a woman in your life who could use a little daily TLC. — Katie McPherson, Associate Editor

Yes, this is a splurge. But it's also SO COOL, and the whole family gets to enjoy it. I was lucky enough to get to try one out for its launch, and it is so fun to program for adults and kids. I love sending my kids a message when I'm away on work trips, but it's also fun to post inspirational sayings, the weather, and daily events or tasks. — Sarah Aswell, Deputy Editor

For the husband who has a watch he loves but a band that has seen better days, this is the upgrade that makes the whole thing feel brand new. Barton’s Genuine Bison leather band is made right here in the USA from real bison leather that is thicker, more textured, and more characterful than standard cowhide, and it only gets better-looking as it breaks in and develops a patina over time. The craftsmanship is genuinely impressive at the price point, it fits most standard watch lugs, and the rich brown tone works with everything from a suit to a flannel. — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social

Splurging on jewelry or perfume is great, but what about splurging on the coziest things possible that can bring you literal comfort on a daily basis? This holiday, you should get someone you love the softest, warmest high-quality blanket that they can lose themselves in this winter. Here's a great pick: this Lux Rabbit throw from Tourance. Yes, it's a little spendier than most blankets, but think about the HOURS you will spend under it, feeling happy. — Sarah Aswell

This set has completely taken over our playroom in the best possible way! Superspace giant magnetic tiles are life-sized building panels made from eco-felt crafted from recycled plastic bottles, and the Family Bundle’s 40 panels give you enough to build actual multi-room forts that kids can crawl inside and play in together. It’s a 2026 National Parenting Product Award winner and a Toy of the Year winner, it’s STEAM accredited, and it’s the kind of open-ended building toy that kids come back to over and over again rather than playing with twice and forgetting about. — Katie Garrity

I am completely obsessed with this jewelry brand; I want all of their stuff! But perhaps my favorite find from them so far is these earrings. Not only do they look stunning on, but they are really easy to put on, never fall off, and are incredibly light for their size. I get compliments every time I wear them, and I always feel just a little more put together when I have them on. I can't wait to try out more of their pieces! — Sarah Aswell

Do you know someone who uses minoxidil (Rogaine)? This is one of those "for the person who has everything" gifts that will genuinely make a little part of their daily life so much better. You fill the chamber with liquid minoxidil and, as you part your hair and run the Rootique device along your head, it sprays it onto your scalp as a fine mist. As someone who's been using Rogaine for over a year, dotting the foam on my scalp with a makeup brush and having the liquid kind run onto my face when I use the dropper, this way of applying it just works so. Much. Better. — Katie McPherson

My sister-in-law decided last year to invest in a really nice camera instead of paying for kid portraits year after year, and it has gone so well for her. She does "shoots" whenever the families get together and the pictures look so professional. She uses her Canon for Christmas cards and birthdays, and she inspired me to do the same thing. I love a gift that keeps on giving every time you use it. And while it's spendy compared to some other items, it can save you in the long run. — Sarah Aswell

I'm at a time when I'm trying to thoughtfully build a little library for myself... and this splurge felt so good as a gift for myself. These books are so beautiful and fun, and the text is still roomy and easy to read. These are books I know I'll read again and again, so they're truly worth it to add to my collection. These are also great gifts for basically any reader that you love. — Sarah Aswell

This tote is a genuine splurge and worth every single penny! The Frances Valentine Crescent in red crinkled leather is the kind of bag that makes an entire outfit without trying, because a red leather tote in this silhouette is simultaneously classic and completely unexpected. The crinkled leather gets more beautiful with every use, the structured crescent shape is roomy enough to actually function as a real daily bag, and the quality is the kind you feel the moment you pick it up. — Katie Garrity

A new mattress topper is always a splurge, but this is the one that makes it feel less painful, because Brooklyn Bedding built it with copper-infused memory foam for pressure relief and zoned lumbar support right where your back needs it. It’s made with CertiPUR-US certified foams, ships to your door, and has a sleep trial so you can actually test it in your own bedroom before committing. Waking up without a sore back is a gift to yourself that you’ll feel every single morning! — Katie Garrity

At $299, this is a real splurge, but it’s the kind of treat-yourself buy I keep going back to. It combines traditional gua sha with red light, infrared light, and soothing vibration, so a single 10-minute session is designed to sculpt, lift, and brighten your face with the press of one button. It’s rechargeable and easy to clean, and it’s from the New York acupuncture studio behind the ORA Method, which makes it feel like a spa facial you can do on the couch. — Katie Garrity

Yes, this is a splurge, but hear me out: You're getting a very cute piece of furniture that will get used every day and that will make your house look cozier and more put together. I love these chairs because they look great but they are actually also comfortable to sit in. So hard to find! And the swivel function is a delight. This fit perfectly into my reading nook and looks great with a fuzzy throw over it. — Sarah Aswell

I’m calling these a splurge because a big set of artist-grade alcohol markers is the kind of thing you hold off on buying for yourself. Each marker has a flexible brush tip and a soft chisel tip, and the alcohol ink blends smoothly without smudging, so you can go from quick coloring to fine detail without switching pens. The ink is refillable, the brush tips are replaceable, and the curved anti-slip barrel is designed for long sessions, which makes these a gift to yourself that actually lasts. — Katie Garrity

Moms don't want a robe for Christmas; we want to embroider a robe for Christmas. This is such a splurgey gift, but... it's one of those gifts that will keep on giving after you realize all it can do. This model comes with over 300 built-in designs as well as 19 different stitches. It also doubles as a traditional sewing machine so that your craft area doesn't get too crowded. Gifting this to the crafty person in your life will not be a mistake. — Sarah Aswell

At $79.99, this is a legit splurge for a power bank, but it’s the one that finally lets me stop carrying a tangle of cords; it snaps magnetically onto my phone and charges wirelessly at up to 15W, and it’s less than half an inch thick. It also has a built-in USB-C cable with a Lightning adapter, a digital battery display, and a 360° kickstand, so I can prop up my phone and keep charging while I watch something or take a call. — Katie Garrity

Tieks makes my #1 favorite ballet flat, so when I heard that they were announcing a new indoor cashmere slipper, I just had to try them. And they did not disappoint! They are so delicate and soft and warm (without being hot) that I feel like a little winter fairy pit-patting around my house in them. And they have the same high quality (and blue soles) as their traditional flats. I know getting mom slippers for Christmas can get a little tired, but the stereotype is for a good reason! — Sarah Aswell

#7917. Getting Answers from ER DVM Courtney Deer

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

If youâve seen The Pitt, youâve got an idea of what happens behind the scenes in an emergency vet hospital. Thereâs always another case to see, another owner to talk to, another patient to check up on. The biggest difference is that we donât often refer things. The initial emergency clinician is also the one assessing the radiographs, interpreting bloodwork, performing surgeries, and managing hospitalized cases. Itâs not uncommon for me to have a critical ICU patient Iâm managing at the same time as Iâm working up an ear infection, or about to go into surgery for a C-section.

Anyone who walks through the ER doors gets triaged, and I see what I can. This can be ear infections, severe dog bite wounds, or behavioral issues.

The most rewarding part of working in emergency veterinary medicine? When the patient is feeling good enough to try to bite you!

Initially, I wasnât sure if I wanted to go to veterinary school. I worked in a boarding clinic attached to a general practice that occasionally let me help on the medicine side, but I wasnât sold on vet med. I didnât get into veterinary school my first application round, so I found a job at a local emergency clinic. My working interview was so wild, I realized Iâd found my passion!

Emergencies come in waves! Some days are âDiarrhea Day,â where everything that comes in has diarrhea. I had âUrine Dayâ last week! By far, Iâd say GI upsets (vomiting, diarrhea, not eating) are the most common ER cases.

Seizures, protracted vomiting, severe weakness. I think anything that comes on suddenly should be investigated quickly!

If youâre worried, Iâm worried. You know your pet best, and if you feel something is âoffâ â donât wait! Even if itâs just for an exam or to get vitals, itâs well worth the peace of mind.

Itâs totally okay to be open about your budget and what you can and cannot do. The ER tends to be more expensive than a daytime practice, and we acknowledge that.  Our job is not to judge; itâs to help! If that means stabilizing until your vet can see you in a few hours, letâs do that.

I saw a lot of disinformation online. I figured if I was louder, I could drown out the bad advice.

I try to time my posts with real-world presentations. Heat stroke cases in the summer, toxicities around the holidays. Sometimes I just have a really interesting case, and I share it right then and there.

That veterinarians are humans too! I post a lot of information for other veterinary professionals, and I hope pet owners see the comments and realize how engaged the community is. Here is a group of people talking about vet med on their day off, learning about cases and new studies, and trying to keep up to date on the latest medicine.

Veterinary medicine is very science-focused. While we are always learning, thereâs a sort of structure to it that doesnât allow for much movement. My books are a whole different part of my brain, one where I can be creative and silly and make up worlds!

âAnother Damn Rescueâ is a spicy shifter romcom where a veterinarian finds an injured âdogâ on the side of the road, only to realize heâs a wolf shifter. Itâs ultimately a love letter to vet med, where I talk about the struggles we face, while also showing the humor and humanity. Oh, and how amazing veterinary technicians, assistants, and receptionists are!

Itâs more of a good time, kick your feet up and giggle sort of story! Pet owners might gain some insight into what itâs like to work in vet med in 2026. Veterinary professionals will enjoy seeing themselves accurately represented in media with a happy ever after!

The podcast is an extension of my social media â itâs a resource for other vets when theyâre not sure where to go. Itâs mostly focused on education for other veterinarians. I bring on specialists and let them pick a topic they feel passionate about. Think of it as continuing education.

Bridging my author identity with my veterinary one is very scary, but also very cool! Iâm especially excited about the podcast because I hope to get companies to talk about new products before they launch as well.

Fatigue! Thereâs compassion and ethical fatigue, where we feel helpless in the face of obstacles outside our reach. Some days I think, âI didnât help anyone today.â And thatâs not true; itâs the story we tell ourselves when weâre in that headspace.

Sometimes we need to take a step back and remember that this is that person's worst day. Ultimately, the team is there to help you. While we donât tolerate abuse, we TOTALLY UNDERSTAND being upset, overwhelmed, having decision paralysis, and everything else that goes along with these scary situations!

I am a pet owner as well as a veterinarian, and Iâve had cases that hit me as a pet owner as well. âIâve been in your shoes before,â goes a long way for owners in these situations. Weâre often told not to interject our opinions, but I am quick to tell owners that Iâve had a pet in the same situation.

Keep ALL of your records! Ask your vet to email you bloodworkand keep it in a folder. Take pictures of your pet's medications. Walking into the ER and saying âHereâs Fluffyâs last bloodworkâ and âhereâs the medication Fluffy is onâ is SO valuable!

XYLITOL!! It can cause fatal low blood sugar and liver damage. Itâs in sugar-free gum, and lately theyâve been calling it âbirch sugar,â so not a lot of people realize itâs the same thing.

Good mentorship is worth its weight in gold! Even the best veterinary school on the planet will not prepare you to step right into an ER without assistance. Ask for help, and find people who are willing to help you learn.

You can find Dr Courtney Deer on Instagram: @er.dvm.

#7916. Rachael Leigh Cook Talks Her New Hallmark Rom-Com, Parenting Teens & 'She's All That'

The Double Booked for the Holidays star (and mom of two) opens up about being in the parenting-a-teen trenches with the rest of us.

For a whole generation of us, Rachael Leigh Cook will forever be Laney Boggs walking down those stairs in *the* red dress. But these days, in addition to being a busy working actor, she’s also a mom of a 13-year-old and an 11-year-old, which means she’s living through the tween and teen years like the rest of us. (“Mixed job performance reviews from my 13-year-old, for sure,” she admits.) And, yep, her daughter has even seen Cook’s iconic ‘90s movies like She’s All That. Her review? She’s glad her mom’s eyebrows grew back.

Also like so many of us, Cook’s a total sucker for a cozy holiday rom-com. It just so happens she’s currently starring in one: Double Booked for the Holidays, now streaming on Hallmark+. She plays identical twins Abigail and Charlie, who head to Wales to a bookish Airbnb for their first Christmas after losing their mom.

When we caught up with Cook, she filled us in on playing double duty, the “say yes” theory that led her to her boyfriend, and the ‘90s icons she considers go-to comfort watches.

Scary Mommy: You're playing twins, which means you're your own scene partner. Which sister is more you, Abigail or Charlie?

Rachael Leigh Cook: I think our producers thought of Abigail as the sort of anchor character in the story. Her love story gets a little bit more screen time, but I just related a lot more to the Charlie character. So that sort of just felt a little easier to latch onto and to have fun with because I'm always just trying to have the best time. When you make these movies, I feel like the audience's enjoyment is my responsibility. If the scene is informational, I'm going to try to make it go fast for you. If it could be a little bit silly, I'm going to make it as silly as they let me. I want it to be fun for you. So when I got to be Charlie and I felt like I got to deliver a little bit more razzle dazzle or whatever you want to call it, that's what felt the best.

SM: What did you do to make the twins feel different? Because I literally had to keep reminding myself there are not, in fact, two of you.

RLC: Julie, that's the nicest thing that you could say. That's what I was utterly terrified of. I read the script, and I thought, Uh-oh, this is going to just seem like I'm talking to myself if I'm not careful because I'm very guilty of being a multi-screen viewer. I'm not afraid to look at my phone. Those shows where if someone just looks at someone and it means something and then you don't understand the next scene, I'm lost. I can't handle it. So I knew that for people like me who might also drift off and just get a snack, I needed everything to be clear. I couldn't have people dipping in and out and feeling confused. This is a holiday movie. We're not trying to confuse anyone.

I really just tried to separate vocally and work from the top of my vocal range to the basement. And that's a little bit difficult because I realized that at the top I can't project very well. But other than that, I feel like it worked pretty well. I just tried to separate the physicality as much as I could so that people weren't confused. We realized that just because of the quick schedule we're on, I couldn't even change hair between the two very much. I got concerned pretty early on that it was just going to be a giant melting pot of too much of me, and that seemed just real bad. So I thought I got to just separate them as much as I can. And if I'm bad, I'm bad, but no one's confused.

SM: You once said something I loved, which is that you’re happiest to be alive when you're living wholly unique experiences.

SM: Did Christmas in a Welsh bookshop movie count?

RLC: Absolutely. I didn't even read the whole script before I said yes. I probably shouldn't admit that, but I just thought no one's going to call and ask if I want to play my own twin ever again in Wales. I can figure out the rest. I'll be fine. This is a say yes moment if there ever was one.

SM: For sure. Any other recent examples that made that list?

RLC: It was I think a little over a year and a half ago, but I remember this day because I got two back-to-back emails. And, listen, most days as an actor are things like, Yeah, they don't want you for that part or Oh, here's a two-cent residual check or whatever. It ain't all glamor.

But one day I got two back-to-back emails and one of them said, "Do you want to be a guest on Name That Tune?" And the other one right after it said, "Do you want to be in a float in the Hollywood Christmas Parade?" And I just wrote, "Yes, send, yes, send." And before I knew it, I had two completely wild experiences because of those things. Because of one of them, I met my now boyfriend, and because of the other one, I got to go and play Name That Tune with Michelle Williams from Destiny's Child.

So that was a pretty awesome validation of my say yes theory.

SM: I am obsessed with everything you just said. Also, that sounds like its own little mini Hallmark movie — you met your boyfriend?! Come on.

RLC: I mean, Hallmark can do just about no wrong as far as I'm concerned. They provide so much cortisol-free entertainment for people with wildly stressful jobs and lives, and I'm all about it. I'm drinking that Kool-Aid all day.

SM: Me too, sister. Well, I want to dip into some nostalgia because we actually recently put your She's All That dress on our list of pop culture dresses we were all obsessed with growing up. You’ve said it didn’t really change you, but rather it revealed your confidence. Do you have a real-life article of clothing that does that for you now?

RLC: I almost don't want to draw attention to it because I know that you'll then see how many times I've worn this. I have this great tracksuit by... Oh my gosh, I can't remember. Why can't I even remember who makes it? I got it in New York. It's sort of cranberry colored. It has stripes on the sleeves. I can get this information to you. And it's matching pants and a top, and there's almost nowhere that this set can't go because you can wear it with heels and some big jewelry and it feels very sort of casual, upscale, athleisure, or you can wear it with sneakers and no extra anything and it just looks like you put some thought into it.

That is my I don't know what to wear outfit. Everyone should have one of those.

SM: Oh, 100%. Well, I know you're in the thick of the tween and early teen years. I have a 13-year-old and a 15-year-old, so we're in it. Number one: how are you?

RLC: Thank you for asking. I think I'm doing fine, but yeah, mixed job performance reviews from my 13-year-old, for sure. I sometimes just feel like I can do no right, and it's really difficult. I'm trying to take what my friends with older kids say about, Oh, it's just because they feel so safe with you that they can just live as their frustrated self, and then they go to school and they behave well and toe the line and all of that. So I'm just like, yep, I'm so honored, so honored. It's a bumpy ride over here, but it's also the very best, and I wouldn't change a thing about it.

I'm absolutely horrified because I can see almost the first break of dawn's light far in the distance of them wanting to leave my home, and that is totally unacceptable. I'm like, "No, you have to stay my babies forever." My son is 11 and still doesn't love sleeping with all the lights off, so I'm hopeful that I can feel like I'm still the mom to a young child in some small ways anyway.

SM: Like you said, it's very day-to-day, so we're just rolling with it. But it's also cool to get to see more of who they're becoming, which I think is really fun.

RLC: Very well said. That's the incredible part. Even though it's the worst thing ever when those memory photos show up on your phone of them as a baby — it's painful because you can't have that time anymore — it's like, "Well, yeah, but I also didn't know you as well."

SM: Exactly. Your daughter, Charlotte, is 13 now… has she watched She’s All That or Josie and the Pussycats yet?

RLC: She has. And they came with me to a screening of Josie at the Hollywood Forever Cemetery pretty recently, and there were, I think, 4,000 people there. It was a big group, and I feel really grateful to them and the revival houses because I don't know if in this day and age there's any chance that my kids would be able to experience work I've done on that scale ever again. I think the kids were mostly in it for the candy, but they were very respectful.

I think my daughter said she's glad my eyebrows grew back, and so am I.

SM: Kids… they sure know how to keep you humble! Last question: As a ‘90s and early ‘00s icon, you’re a comfort watch for a lot of us.

SM: I’m curious, what is your comfort watch?

RLC: Oh, man. I geeked out over... I met Elizabeth Shue one time. I can't tell you how many times I've seen Adventures in Babysitting. So someone like that. I've never met Molly Ringwald, but I would be the least cool human in the world. I grew up on John Hughes movies and her. So yeah, I'd say those.

SM: I love it. You’ve been a true joy, and it's such an honor to meet you.

RLC: Mine! And you're doing great. You really are.

SM: You too. We’ll get to the other side of all this; we will.

SM: Oh, babe, that’s a convo for a whole other interview.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

#7914. Her friend died after giving birth. Now she’s writing legislation to save other moms

Home / Health & Wellness / Women's Health

By Cassie Shortsleeve Updated Nov. 24, 2026

Mothering America is a regular column from Motherly and Chamber of Mothers sharing moms’ stories from across the country, showing the power of coming together to make change. Each piece is part of a larger effort to ensure every mother and family in the U.S. has the support and care to be well.

In 2008, Lauren Underwood was in graduate school at Johns Hopkins, earning a master’s in public health, when she met a woman with a big, bright smile named Shalon Irving.

She never would have imagined the impact that friendship would have on her life’s work. Underwood would eventually become a U.S. representative for the state of Illinois, fighting to protect moms like Irving, who died before she could see her friend take office.

At the time, Irving, who already had her PhD, was coming back to school for additional training in public health. “We were just like regular girlfriends, passing notes in class and everything,” Rep. Underwood says.

The two—Rep. Underwood, a registered nurse, and Irving, an epidemiologist—stayed in touch through the years. In January 2017, Rep. Underwood served as a senior advisor at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, and Irving worked for the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). She had also given birth to a beautiful baby girl named Soleil.

Three weeks later, though, Irving wasn’t feeling well. “She went to the doctor several times, explaining that something wasn’t right,” Rep. Underwood remembers. On January 28, Irving died of complications related to high blood pressure. She was 36.

“Shalon had a career focused on ending health disparities, and she was so excited to become a mom,” Rep. Underwood says.

Today, Rep. Underwood is the architect of a series of 14 bills called the Momnibus, which was reintroduced to Congress this spring. The Momnibus addresses “every clinical and non-clinical factor” leading to preventable maternal deaths and disparities in this country; it’s evidence-based, data-driven, and offers states, communities, providers, and nonprofits the resources to help save moms like Irving’s lives. For Rep. Underwood, the Momnibus is personal.

While a member of Congress, Rep. Underwood is also a woman and a friend who, like too many in this country, lost a dear friend and felt a fire to make change.

Rep. Underwood recalls Irving’s funeral as devastating—particularly because many of those in attendance held positions of the highest authority in public health in this country. She remembers the head of the CDC speaking at Irving’s funeral and expressing bewilderment at her death.

For Rep. Underwood, it was no mystery why mothers like Irving die in childbirth and shortly thereafter. As a clinician, she had seen firsthand health disparities in action; as a Black woman, maternal mortality was an unfortunate “phenomenon where it’s just so common when you talk about the maternal crisis.”

Today, we know about 84 percent of pregnancy-related deaths like Irving’s are preventable—meaning that most of the moms who aren’t here today should be here, and could be here, with the proper supports in place. Black moms are more than three times as likely to die in pregnancy or the postpartum months than white women—a disparity that persists across income and education levels.

“People think higher education or higher income is protective. They think that if you are a healthcare worker, you’re going to get the best healthcare. If you know the risks, are self-aware, confident, and have agency, and you can speak up for yourself, then these kinds of things won’t happen to you. Shalon and her death fly in the face of all of those assumptions, and it breaks your heart.”

When she made the decision to run for Congress, Rep. Underwood knew that if she won, maternal mortality would be an issue she’d work on.

In 2018, Rep. Underwood became the youngest Black woman ever elected to Congress. She teamed up with Rep. Alma Adams (D-NC), who also had personal experience with maternal health: Adams’ daughter had experienced a very challenging labor and delivery, known in medical terms as severe maternal morbidity, or an experience that has lasting impacts on a mother’s health.

Together, in April 2019, the two formed the Black Maternal Health Caucus. At a crowded press conference, Rep. Underwood fought back tears. “To be in this moment with the dome of the Capitol behind us and these cameras and people asking questions and it’s this diverse, multi-generational, multi-ethnic, male and female moment of speaking about an issue that was so personal to me—I was just overcome,” she says. “It was a moment of power and resolve. It was an invitation. We were planting a flag, saying, ‘We’re here. We’re going to do this work. We know that there’s an opportunity to bring change.’”

Rep. Underwood didn’t expect the Black Maternal Health Caucus to grow into one of the largest bipartisan caucuses on the Hill. “We left that press conference and our phones started ringing, and it never stopped.”

Rep. Underwood has dedicated her career to ensuring everyone—moms included—has equitable healthcare so we can all feel our best. She’s also dedicated her career to ending the maternal mortality crisis. “We know exactly what to do. We just need to invest, have the resolve, and to say, ‘This is unacceptable. Let’s fix this issue.’”

She also reminds us that Congress works on the issues that members raise. “If a Member comes in and says, ‘This is important to my community, and this is an essential issue that we tackle,’ that’s how solutions advance.” Many of her ideas for bills, she says, come from your stories.

“Often, people think that their story doesn’t matter, and when they come in to advocate, they think they need to have statistics or be a walking encyclopedia,” Rep. Underwood says. “But we are in a relationship business, and connection is currency. The fastest way to build a connection is to share your humanity, tell your story, and invite space for that vulnerability.”

What that means for you: If you have a story to share, Members of Congress are home in their districts through the end of the month, with offices open Monday through Friday and available for meetings. (Not sure how to set up a meeting? Check out Chamber of Mothers’ ‘Moms at Recess’ guide, which includes step-by-step plans and tips for hosting a meeting with Members of Congress.)

Rep. Underwood also underscores the importance of being loud about solutions and progress in maternal health. She highlights the power of doulas, lactation consultants, and community support in maternal health—and the fact that, to date, one of the Momnibus’ 14 bills has been signed into law. Others have passed the House. The Momnibus has also unlocked more than $250 million for states, community organizations, researchers, and providers to save lives. (You can find out which projects are being funded with Momnibus dollars in your community through the Caucus’s Momnibus Money Tracker.)

“We want the news of a pregnancy to be a time of joy and hope and eager anticipation and wonder,” Rep. Underwood says. “This can’t just be a conversation around problems. We want people to know that we’re working on this, that we have their backs, and about the opportunities, help, and the resources that are available.”

#7913. Diapers & Eczema: What Dermatologists Say

Here’s how to tell the difference, and which sensitive-skin diapers are worth buying.

It’s 11 p.m. You’re standing by the crib after changing a diaper, hyper-focused on the glaring rash shining up at you. You’re frantically trying to Google symptoms, causes, and solutions just to soothe your baby’s bottom. Now you've got an arsenal of tabs open and are wondering if this is something you caused.

You didn’t. And for what it's worth, your baby’s butt rash is not a referendum on your parenting. Skin trouble in the diaper area is very common (ugh), but it’s very manageable once you know what you’re dealing with (whew!).

Here’s what you actually need to focus on, minus any panic-inducing packaging jargon.

All your internet sleuthing raises another question: Is it diaper rash or eczema? Three different things can pop up under a diaper:

Why is eczema a big deal down there? Eczema-prone skin means a weaker barrier, so the constant moisture and friction of a diaper can irritate it faster and more severely.

Babies have a much thinner skin barrier than adults, which is why, per the AAP, more than half of babies get diaper rash at some point. [1] A diaper puts baby's skin up against three things:

Spoiler alert: Words like “gentle” and “natural” aren’t regulated. Here’s what to actually look for:

The following habits are vital, per the AAP: [1]

A note on steroid creams: The AAP says that for infant eczema flares, a low-potency topical corticosteroid such as hydrocortisone 1% or 2.5% is typically sufficient. Mid-potency steroids should generally be avoided in the diaper area because occlusion increases absorption. But always check with your pediatrician before using any steroid cream on your baby. [4]

Sometimes a simple diaper swap won’t do the trick. Here are common signs it’s time to call a pediatrician or dermatologist: [1]

Pampers is the only brand we found with two kinds of third-party validation across its sensitive-skin line. The newest, Pampers AMORE, is dermatologically accredited by the Skin Health Alliance and tested against more than 1,000 chemicals, according to Pampers’ product specifications. It’s hypoallergenic and free of fragrance, parabens, elemental chlorine, and latex. [5] Pampers Pure Protection carries the National Eczema Association’s Seal of Acceptance. [6] Pampers Swaddlers went fully fragrance-free across all sizes on June 22, 2026. [3] They are dermatologically tested and accredited by the Skin Health Alliance.

According to DYPER, the materials that touch baby’s skin are 100% plant-based, and the diaper has 55% USDA Certified Biobased content and is dermatologist-tested. [7]

Per Bambo Nature, the fluff pulp is totally chlorine-free (TCF), and the diapers contain no added substances known to be allergens or classified as skin irritants. [8]

Huggies says Snug & Dry diapers are entirely fragrance-free, as well as free of lotions, parabens, and natural rubber latex. [9]

Per Honest, these diapers are OEKO-TEX Standard 100 certified (third-party tested for 350 harmful substances), dermatologist-tested, hypoallergenic, and fragrance-free. [10]

What are the best diapers for a baby with sensitive skin? Look for diapers that are fragrance-free, hypoallergenic, and dermatologist-tested, ideally with third-party accreditation. Pampers Swaddlers (fragrance-free across all sizes since June 2026), Pampers Pure Protection (National Eczema Association Seal of Acceptance), and Pampers AMORE (Skin Health Alliance-accredited) all meet those criteria.

What diapers do pediatric dermatologists recommend for sensitive or reactive skin? Rather than marketing words like “gentle” or “natural,” dermatologists prioritize independent validation, such as Skin Health Alliance accreditation or the National Eczema Association Seal of Acceptance. Those marks mean an outside organization has reviewed the product.

What’s the best hypoallergenic diaper for a baby with eczema? The National Eczema Association’s Seal of Acceptance is the clearest outside marker for eczema-prone skin and, according to the NEA, Pampers Pure Protection currently carries it.

What’s the best sensitive-skin diaper of 2026 for a baby with eczema? Pampers AMORE is the newest diaper built specifically for sensitive skin. Per Pampers, it’s accredited by the Skin Health Alliance, tested against more than 1000 chemicals, and free of fragrance, parabens, elemental chlorine, and latex.

Can switching diapers alone fix my baby’s eczema? No. A fragrance-free, hypoallergenic diaper helps, but routine matters as much or more: change every two to three hours, use barrier cream at every change, give daily diaper-free time, and clean gently. And since eczema is a chronic condition, your pediatrician should be part of the plan.

Why does my baby’s rash only show up near the diaper elastic or leg cuffs? That pattern suggests a contact allergy to dye or elastic material rather than just general dermatitis. Have your pediatrician take a look.
