#7881. Better a Bald Head Than a Cat That’s Dead: This Common Hair Growth Formula Is Killing Pets

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Humans have a rather complex and contradictory relationship with their hair. Many of us willingly put ourselves through torturous procedures to remove it from our legs, armpits, and just about anywhere else, while, at the same time, the quest to keep a full and lustrous head of hair fuels a billion-dollar hair growth industry. Since the 1980s, a chemical called Minoxidil has become increasingly popular as both a topical and oral treatment for baldness, but what few people realize is that the very product promising hair growth poses a serious risk to their pets. The American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) is warning consumers about minoxidil toxicity in cats and dogs, highlighting a danger that deserves considerably more attention.

Anyone who shares a home with a cat knows that personal space is more of a suggestion than a household rule. Cats rub against our heads, groom our hair, curl up on our pillows, and somehow manage to investigate just about everything we touch. These perfectly normal feline behaviors can turn deadly when minoxidil enters the picture.

The history of minoxidil shares similarities with another well-known human drug: Viagra, which essentially took a common side effect of the heart medication, sildenafil, and turned it into its primary purpose. In the 1970s, researchers developing a new blood pressure medication found that a common side effect of the drug, minoxidil, was hypertrichosis, aka excessive hair growth. Like the story of sildenafil, the makers of minoxidil leaned into this side effect, repurposing the drug as a treatment for hair loss.1

In 1988, the FDA officially approved minoxidil, and it quickly gained popularity in products like Rogaine. Minoxidil works by widening blood vessels, a process called vasodilation, and altering the hair growth cycle to stimulate hair growth. But what helps us fight hair loss can be dangerous for our feline roommates.

A 2021 study published in the Journal of the American Animal Hospital Association examined 211 reported cases of topical minoxidil exposure in dogs and cats. Of the 87 animals that developed signs of poisoning, 62 were cats, and 25 were dogs. Eight cats died. A 2025 review in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology identified another 94 reported cases, including 68 cats, ten of which died. Notably, 55 of 57 cases involving accidental exposure to a person's minoxidil treatment involved cats.

How does this happen? Topical minoxidil is applied directly to the scalp, either as a liquid using a dropper or as a foam spread with the fingers. Medication can remain on the hands, hair, or nearby surfaces. Cats don't need to break into the medicine cabinet; a little grooming, an affectionate head rub, or a snooze on a contaminated pillow may be enough to expose them. Some were even exposed through everyday contact with their follicle-challenged cat parents.

Minoxidil works by relaxing blood vessels and improving blood flow. In cats, however, the effects can become dangerously disruptive.

When absorbed, it can cause blood pressure to drop dramatically, a condition called hypotension. To compensate, the heart beats faster, but this doesn't necessarily solve the problem. Serious complications can follow, including fluid accumulation in the lungs (pulmonary edema) or in the space surrounding them (pleural effusion). Breathing becomes increasingly difficult, and severe poisoning can progress to cardiovascular and respiratory failure.

Now, what should you look out for? You might notice unusual tiredness, weakness, vomiting, or a sudden loss of appetite. More concerningly, your kitty may start breathing faster than usual or appear to struggle for air. And here's the tricky part: some cats may initially seem perfectly fine.

That's why a suspected exposure should never be brushed off simply because your cat appears normal. Waiting for visible signs of poisoning can waste valuable time.

Now that we are beginning to appreciate the risks this product poses to our pets, we have to wonder how many unexplained cat and dog deaths could be attributed to unknown minoxidil exposure.

Rapunzel may have had a tower to keep her hair safe, but cat owners need a different strategy: keeping minoxidil well away from curious paws.

If you use topical minoxidil, make sure you apply it in a room your cat cannot access. Wash your hands thoroughly with soap and water immediately afterward, and clean up any spills promptly. Used tissues, cotton pads, applicators, and empty containers should go straight into a secure bin. That tissue you casually leave on the bathroom counter? To your cat, it might look like just another interesting thing to investigate.

And what about bedtime? If you apply minoxidil in your bedroom, make closing the door part of your nighttime routine. Your cat may protest being left out of the bedroom, especially if your pillow is their favorite sleeping spot, but keeping them away from treated hair, skin, pillows, and bedding can help prevent accidental contact with medication residue. Remember, allowing the product to dry does not guarantee that every surface is free from contamination.

You might be wondering whether switching to oral minoxidil would solve the problem. Unfortunately, not entirely. Oral minoxidil is also toxic to cats if they accidentally ingest a tablet. Whichever formulation you use, keep the medication securely stored and well out of paws' reach. Or better yet, look into options that donât put your pet at risk.

Discuss your household's furry residents with the prescribing dermatologist and establish a routine that prevents accidental exposure. Cats are wonderfully persistent creatures. They may not appreciate a closed door or understand why their favorite pillow is suddenly off-limits, but a little inconvenience is a small price to pay for keeping them safe.

If your cat licks minoxidil, contacts a spill, or may have groomed contaminated fur, contact your veterinarian or an animal poison control service immediately, even if your kitty seems perfectly fine.

Treatment depends on the exposure and your cat's condition. It may involve hospitalization, cardiovascular monitoring, oxygen therapy, intravenous support, and medications to manage complications such as low blood pressure or fluid accumulation.

Never attempt to induce vomiting or administer home remedies unless specifically instructed by a veterinary professional. If medication is still on your cat's coat or skin, ask your veterinarian how to handle decontamination safely rather than delaying emergency care.

Unfortunately, not every cat survives minoxidil poisoning, making every accidental exposure a veterinary emergency.

hhttps://www.instagram.com/reel/DeF7upKOC-1/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&dmpr=NTc4MTIwNjQ2YQ==

Hair loss can affect confidence, and wanting to treat it is perfectly understandable. Minoxidil can be a valuable treatment for people experiencing certain types of hair loss, but sharing a home with a cat adds an important responsibility.

Preventing accidental poisoning starts with awareness. As pet parents, we need to be mindful of the products we bring into our homes, even those that seem perfectly harmless to us. From seemingly innocent houseplants and everyday foods to cleaning products, medications, and personal care treatments, many things we use routinely can pose risks to our feline companions. Before introducing something new into your home, take a moment to consider whether it is safe for your cat. A little research and a few precautions can make a world of difference.

Cats will continue doing what cats do best: following their humans, investigating everything, claiming the pillows, and showing affection on their own terms. We cannot expect them to understand why a particular patch of skin or a freshly treated pillow is suddenly off-limits. That responsibility belongs to us.

Thinning hair can be frustrating, even damaging to self-esteem, but itâs not a life-threatening condition. Losing a beloved pet to an avoidable medication exposure is a tragedy no one should have to experience.

Better bald than catless. Every single time.

#7879. Turkey and Gravy and Pumpkin - Oh My! What Cats Can and Can’t Eat at Thanksgiving

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Cats are famously persistent beggars, and a holiday table full of tempting smells gives them plenty of motivation. Although there are a handful of Thanksgiving dishes that are fine in small amounts, several can make a cat seriously ill, so it pays to know which is which before anything gets shared.

The following foods are generally harmless for cats, provided the portions stay small and there are no pre-existing health complications. Of course, safe doesnât always mean healthy, and moderation is key. Just like people, cats also differ in what they like, and many will show no interest in some of these at all.

Plain turkey is the best choice, since cats are obligate carnivores and tend to love it. It needs to be free of skin, fat, bones, gravy, and spices, and a small piece is plenty. The best thing to do is set aside a small amount to cook without all the frills, rather than cleaning it later.

Plain, cooked pumpkin is non-toxic and good for a catâs digestion, and it may even soothe an upset stomach. A puree or mash works well. Pumpkin pie is a different matter, because the sugar and possible dairy arenât good for cats.

Apples are safe and offer vitamins C and K, calcium, and fiber. The seeds, leaves, and stems contain cyanide and must be removed, and the fruit should be chopped into small cubes.

Plain green beans, minus butter, spices, herbs, onion, or garlic, are a good source of fiber and can even stand in for regular treats. Broccoli is also safe if it is unseasoned and boiled or steamed. Itâs unlikely a cat will want it, but it provides antioxidants and supports digestion. As with any new food, itâs best to introduce it carefully. Cranberry sauce isnât toxic, but its sugar content makes it unhealthy, so only an incredibly small taste is appropriate.

Some Thanksgiving staples should never be shared, because they can make a cat quite ill.

Garlic, onions, leeks, scallions, and similar vegetables can be deadly even in small amounts, and garlic powder is particularly problematic. They damage a catâs red blood cells and lead to anemia, with signs such as weakness, a high heart rate, diarrhea, vomiting, and collapse. Cats are more sensitive to them than dogs, and symptoms have reportedly appeared after less than a teaspoon of cooked onion.

Many stuffings contain onions or garlic. Even without them, stuffing is usually rich with ingredients like turkey grease that can upset a catâs stomach. It wonât be deadly without those ingredients, but it has no nutritional value and can wreak havoc on digestion.

Bones should stay well out of reach. Cooked bones in particular can splinter or crack and could tear the mouth, break teeth, cause choking, or block the digestive system, and bacteria are a concern too. Keep them well out of reach.

Chocolate is incredibly toxic to cats, and the darker it is, the worse it gets. The theobromine and caffeine it contains can cause vomiting, muscle tremors, diarrhea, an abnormal heart rate, and seizures, and it can even lead to death. Anything else with caffeine, including coffee, is off limits as well.

Grapes and raisins can lead to kidney failure, and even a tiny amount of either, or related dried fruits like craisins, can cause illness. Signs include continuous vomiting, stomach distress, and hyperactivity. Some cats show no symptoms after eating them, but that isnât a reason to take the chance.

Gravy isnât toxic, but it is salty and fatty, which cats donât need much of. Those levels could cause further problems for a cat with heart trouble. A sneaky lick is nothing to worry about, but gravy shouldnât be mixed into a catâs food.

A bowl of milk may seem harmless, but many cats are lactose intolerant. Dairy can give them a stomach ache, gas, or diarrhea, so itâs better to offer something from the safe list instead if theyâre sniffing around the kitchen.

Raw meat and fish can carry pathogens such as E. coli and Salmonella that make cats ill, so avoid the temptation to drop some scraps as youâre preparing meals.

A cat can share in the holiday with a nibble of plain turkey or a spoonful of pumpkin, but a few ordinary ingredients you may have around the table can cause illness and even death. With a little care over what goes into the bowl, both cat and family can enjoy a safe and happy Thanksgiving.

#7878. When a Pet's Final Goodbye Becomes a Nightmare: The Philippines Crematorium Scandal

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

For families who have just lost a beloved pet, arranging cremation is often one of the last acts of love they can offer. They choose a service, pay for the arrangements, and believe that their companion will be treated with dignity and respect. They may never see what happens behind the crematorium doors, but they trust that their furry family member is in caring hands.

Sadly, for hundreds of families in the Philippines, that trust has been destroyed.

What began as a neighborhood concern over a foul smell quickly turned into a disturbing discovery. On October 29, 2026, residents of Barangay Minuyan in San Jose del Monte, Bulacan, were disturbed by a strong, suffocating, and foul odor coming from a nearby vacant lot. The terrible stink prompted a report and closer inspection, leading to the nightmare-worthy discovery of seven large sacks containing the remains of 26 dogs and three cats; each one wrapped in plastic bags bearing identification labels with their names and weights.

The investigation eventually led to Ahjay Paws Aftercare Pet Crematorium in Bacoor, Cavite, where many families had entrusted their deceased pets for cremation.

By November 4, authorities had recovered 29 animal carcasses, while 20 containers of ashes surrendered by families were undergoing forensic examination. The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) is investigating possible fraud and other violations, and at least 250 pet owners have reportedly filed complaints against the company.

The questions are heartbreaking. Were these families given the ashes of their own pets? Were some animals never cremated at all? How did companions entrusted to a professional aftercare service end up in plastic bags beside a road?

For grieving pet owners, discovering that their furry family member's final arrangements may have been mishandled is an especially cruel betrayal.

Sadly, this is not the only case, or the only country, where fraud and deception have pervaded what should be a sacred service. In 2025, the Casa XibalbÃ¡ case in Quintana Roo, Mexico, exposed a similarly disturbing situation. Authorities investigating a Chetumal pet crematorium found that families had paid to have their beloved companions cremated, only to receive urns containing soil instead of their pets' ashes. Even worse, more than 180 animal carcasses were reportedly discovered during searches connected with the investigation. The case involved allegations of fraud and improper disposal of animal remains, with legal proceedings continuing into 2026.

Different countries, different businesses, but an eerily similar betrayal. And in both cases, the damage potentially reaches far beyond the families who were deceived.

Another disturbing side of these horrific stories is the environmental impact. Improperly discarded animal remains can create environmental hazards, particularly when several carcasses accumulate in unmanaged locations.

As tissues decompose, bodily fluids and organic material are released. These substances can contribute to leachate, a liquid that may move through soil with rainfall and drainage. Depending on soil conditions, groundwater depth, and proximity to wells or waterways, this can create pathways for environmental contamination.

Biohazardous runoff, odors, and potential groundwater pollution are among the concerns associated with improperly managed animal carcasses. If investigators discover that remains were repeatedly discarded at multiple locations, removing the visible carcasses may not be enough. Surrounding soil, drainage systems, and nearby water sources may also need assessment.

The deceived pet owners deserve justice, but residents also need answers about the conditions around their homes.

Exposed animal remains can attract scavengers, including free-roaming dogs, cats, and wildlife. Insects may also come into contact with decomposing material and potentially spread infectious agents between locations.

Not every deceased animal carries an infectious disease, and finding carcasses does not automatically mean disease will spread. However, when the cause of death is unknown, there may be no way to determine whether the remains contain infectious agents that could expose other animals.

There is another potential hazard that pet owners may not immediately consider: euthanasia medications.

Pentobarbital, commonly used for humane euthanasia in veterinary medicine, can remain in an animal's tissues after death. Wildlife that consumes the remains of an animal euthanized with this drug can suffer secondary poisoning, with scavenging birds being particularly vulnerable.

And this is where the consequences can extend much further. Scavengers play an essential role in maintaining healthy ecosystems by removing animal carcasses before they become sources of environmental contamination and disease transmission. Vultures, for example, can consume remains that might otherwise attract other scavengers or allow infectious agents to persist in the environment. When scavenger populations decline, carcasses can remain accessible for longer, potentially increasing opportunities for pathogen transmission and disease spread.

A carcass that should have been cremated could therefore become a source of danger to another animal. The irony is that the very animals helping keep ecosystems clean could be exposed to a potentially lethal drug simply because someone failed to dispose of a pet's remains responsibly.

The scandals also raise questions about oversight of the pet aftercare industry. A business permit cannot demonstrate that every animal entrusted to a facility has been handled properly.

Families should be able to expect accountability throughout the process, from collection and identification to transportation, cremation, and the return of ashes. Records should establish which animal was received, where it was taken, and what happened to its remains.

The Philippine Animal Welfare Society (PAWS) says the case has also highlighted a potential legal gap. According to the organization, the alleged deception may not fall directly under the Animal Welfare Act because the animals were already deceased when entrusted to the crematorium. However, the alleged conduct may constitute âestafaâ, or fraud by deceit, under the Revised Penal Code.

Affected families have been encouraged to preserve receipts, cremation certificates, photographs, messages, and other documentation that could support their complaints.

The Casa XibalbÃ¡ case in Mexico revealed a similarly disturbing situation, with more than 180 animal carcasses reportedly discovered and families allegedly receiving urns filled with soil instead of their pets' ashes. Two countries, two scandals, and far too many grieving families betrayed by businesses they trusted.

The death of a beloved pet is already a difficult time. Families make end-of-life decisions, discuss euthanasia with their veterinarians, arrange transportation, and decide how they would like to remember their companions.

For some, receiving an urn containing their pet's ashes brings comfort. It becomes something tangible to keep beside a favorite photograph or in a special place at home. And while emotional cost is the most painful aspect for the affected pet owners, itâs also worth noting that individual cremation usually comes at a premium price; a price paid for a service not performed. But regardless of whether these pets were to have undergone individual or commingled cremation, families deserve honesty about the service they purchase.

They should never have to question whether the ashes they brought home belong to their furry family member.

There is something particularly upsetting about the possibility that an animal cherished throughout life, treated as family, and surrounded by affection could have its remains handled so carelessly.

People entrust pet aftercare providers with something deeply personal. They are saying goodbye to someone they loved. That deserves respect.

Your Thanksgiving feast could provide a few tasty treats for garden birds. Just make sure you know which leftovers are safe to serve and which should stay off the menu.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The holidays often leave us with more food than we know what to do with, don't they? Before throwing everything into the compost or bin, though, take a look at your Thanksgiving leftovers; your feathered friends could be very thankful for them!

Yes, some everyday ingredients from the feasting table can make welcome treats for backyard birds, offering a little extra nourishment as temperatures drop and the nights draw in (and transform your outdoor space into a welcoming bird sanctuary in the process).

Whether you're hoping to see your birth month bird out there, or just happy to offer your kitchen scraps up to any local critters who might make use of them, here's how to use your Thanksgiving leftovers to keep bird feeders filled over the holidays...

Before we dive on in, a word of caution: not every Thanksgiving dish is suitable for wildlife, especially as salt, butter, rich sauces and seasonings can make seemingly harmless scraps unsuitable for birds.

The trick? Try to save a few simple ingredients before they make their way into the casserole dish or onto the dinner table. With that caveat in place, then, here are seven Thanksgiving kitchen scraps worth keeping...

Have a few apples left over from your Thanksgiving preparations? Birds such as robins and other fruit-eating visitors will definitely appreciate small pieces of fresh apple.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Cut the flesh into bite-sized chunks, removing the core and seeds first. Bruised apples are fine so long as they're fresh (they're not as fussy as we are!), but discard any mouldy or spoiled pieces. And avoid offering apple pie filling or cooked apples covered in sugar and spices.

Cranberries are a Thanksgiving staple, and you'd better believe that their fresh (and unseasoned, obviously) counterparts make a lovely treat for birds. Offer a few whole or chopped cranberries on a clean feeding tray like this one from MIXXIDEA.

Frozen cranberries are fine, too, once thawed. Just avoid cranberry sauce, as it typically contains added sugar and may include other ingredients birds don't need. Honestly, a little fresh fruit is all that's required.

Pecans (again, plain and unsalted) are another holiday favorite that can be shared with feathered visitors, along with walnuts and peanuts. All of these scrummy nuts are rife at Thanksgiving, and all provide fats and protein that can help birds maintain their energy during colder weather.

Take care to chop larger nuts into manageable pieces and check that they haven't been coated in salt, sugar, chocolate or seasoning. Just like the fruit, nuts should be fresh, too, rather than stale or musty.

Corn often features on the Thanksgiving menu in a big way, and a few plain kernels can be offered to garden birds; just set aside a small portion before adding butter, salt or other seasonings.

Cooked or fresh corn kernels can be placed on a feeding tray, but avoid creamed corn, buttery corn casserole and heavily seasoned dishes. Only offer a little at a time, as damp corn can spoil quickly.

If pumpkin or squash features in your holiday cooking (or your Thanksgiving decor, if you're Kristin Davis!), don't throw away all those seeds; instead, rinse away any stringy pulp, remove any seasoning and allow the seeds to dry thoroughly.

Offer them (have I gotten too repetitive yet?) plain and unsalted, either whole for larger birds or broken into smaller pieces for smaller visitors. They're a useful source of fats and nutrients, making them a worthwhile addition to your bird feeding station.

Leftover rice can also be shared with birds from your Thanksgiving feast, provided it hasn't been cooked with salt, butter, oil, garlic or onions. Both white and brown rice are suitable in small quantities when prepared plainly.

P.S. There's a persistent myth that uncooked or cooked rice swells inside birds and causes harm, but this isn't true. Nevertheless, rice shouldn't replace more nutritious bird food, so just offer just a small amount (you may find your birth month winter bird adores it) and remove anything uneaten so it doesn't have a chance to go bad.

A little leftover boiled or baked potato from your Thanksgiving prep can be another treat for your feathered friends. Set aside a portion before adding butter, milk, salt or gravy, then allow it to cool and chop it into small pieces.

Please never offer raw potatoes or green potato peelings, and avoid chips, roast potatoes cooked in fat and heavily seasoned mashed potatoes. Experts always advise that plain potato be treated as an occasional extra rather than a regular food source.

It's every bit as important to know what to avoid when it comes to feeding birds your Thanksgiving leftovers. Turkey fat and pan drippings might seem like an easy substitute for bird suet, but they're best kept off the feeding station. Audubon, in fact, warns that turkey fat melts more readily than traditional suet and can turn rancid quickly. It can also smear onto feathers, potentially affecting their waterproofing and insulation.

Gravy, stuffing and salty side dishes should also stay off the menu, as they often contain butter, salt, onion and garlic, none of which are suitable additions to a wild bird's diet. Avoid, too, anything that contains chocolate, along with avocado, sugary desserts and heavily processed foods, too. Bread and pastry aren't particularly nutritious (even if they won't do any harm), so think up some better ways to use your leftovers; might this author humbly submit the idea of a bread-and-butter pudding?

Once you've picked all of the bird-friendly scraps out of your Thanksgiving feast, be sure to present it properly! Always use a clean feeding tray rather than leaving piles of food on the ground, and try to put food out in the morning, as this is when it's most likely to be eaten.

Take care to remove anything uneaten before it spoils, and wash feeding surfaces regularly to reduce the risk of bacteria and disease spreading. It's also worth keeping fresh drinking water available, particularly as colder weather approaches, and remember that kitchen scraps are supposed to be occasional extras, not a replacement for a balanced wild bird food mix.

Still, all those warnings aside, there's no denying that sharing a little of your holiday feast with your local birds is a lovely way to give thanks to Mother Nature (and reduce food waste at the same time).

#7875. Paws Off the Stuffing: A Guide to Safe Thanksgiving Foods for Dogs

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Letâs face it: despite its somewhat complicated and controversial history, these days,Thanksgiving is built around food, which makes it one of the trickiest holidays for dogs that want to join you around the table, since many common dishes contain ingredients that are toxic to them. Some foods are fine to share in small amounts, while others can cause anything from an upset stomach to life-threatening illness. Knowing which is which makes it easy to include a dog in the day without risking an emergency.

Turkey is safe and healthy for dogs, with a few conditions. The skin is fatty and usually coated in bastings and spices, and too much fat can lead to obesity and pancreatitis. Turkey bones can splinter and damage a dogâs mouth and digestive tract, so they should be avoided. Seasonings, including salt, can cause toxicity, so processed turkey should be skipped too. Plain meat is the safe choice, with no sauces or gravy.

Plain pumpkin is considered healthy, which is why so many dog foods contain it. Canned or fresh both work, provided the canned kind isnât pre-seasoned and nothing has been added. Pumpkin pie, with its spices and sugar, is a definite no.

Sweet potatoes are full of nutrients and vitamins, but they should be cooked and served in small amounts, without marshmallows, seasoning, or butter. Green beans offer vitamins, fiber, and manganese. They can be steamed, raw, canned, or cooked, as long as they are plain and not part of a casserole.

Corn is healthy without butter or salt, but only if it's been taken off the cob. Corn cobs are a relatively common source of intestinal blockage in dogs. Carrots, celery, and peas are fine cooked or raw and unseasoned, and carrots and celery should be cut into bite-sized pieces to prevent choking.

Plain cranberries are safe in moderation, though cranberry sauce and juice contain too much sugar. If they come from a dried fruit pack, only the cranberries should go to the dog. Apple slices are healthy and tasty, but the core and seeds should go in the trash. The seeds contain small amounts of cyanide that wonât harm a dog unless it eats too many, but itâs best to be cautious. The pie is for the people.

Cheese makes a tasty treat unless a dog is lactose intolerant, and low-fat versions suit dogs watching their weight. A small piece of plain bread is safe unless the dog has a grain allergy. It should have no raisins, seeds, or nuts, and since bread offers few nutritional benefits, it should only be an occasional snack.

Onions are highly toxic to dogs, along with everything in the onion family, including shallots, chives, and leeks, as they can cause anemia and liver damage. Garlic should also be avoided, and garlic powder is especially potent. It can also cause anemia, among other problems, so it shouldnât be anywhere near your pet.

Stuffing is also off limits. It usually contains onion, and it often carries a large amount of butter, which makes it too fatty for a dogâs diet. Mashed potatoes are fine if completely plain, but most are made with plenty of salt, butter, and other ingredients that arenât good for dogs, so itâs best to skip them. Gravy is a problem because of its high sodium, and it usually contains onions or garlic.

Chocolate is toxic because of two chemicals, theobromine and caffeine. It can lead to death if left untreated, and the signs can appear relatively quickly. Caffeinated drinks are risky for the same reason. Dogs are smaller and lighter than people, so it doesnât take much caffeine to cause trouble, and that rules out coffee, tea, and soft drinks.

Yeast-based bread dough is dangerous even though small amounts of baked bread are fine. The yeast expands in a dogâs stomach and can lead to bloat, which can progress to a life-threatening condition called gastric dilatation-volvulus. Alcohol of any kind causes poisoning in dogs, whether itâs a drink, rubbing alcohol, or hand sanitizer.

A final but deadly ingredient to be aware of is the artificial sweetener, xylitol. Sometimes listed as birch sugar, even in small amounts, this seemingly minor ingredient causes severe hypoglycemia, and even if dogs survive this, irreversible liver damage can finish them off. Always keep an eye out for this one, commonly included in sugar-free mints, gums, candy, and peanut butter, to name a few.

A dog caught eating something toxic needs to go straight to a vet or the nearest emergency animal clinic. Bringing the packaging, along with a sample of whatever the dog ingested, helps the vet treat that particular substance. When itâs unclear whether something was toxic, the ASPCA Animal Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 and the Pet Poison Helpline at (855) 764-7661 can help. Both charge a fee, but they can guide the next steps and get a pet immediate help.

When it comes to ingested toxic ingredients, timing is everything. If you know your dog has eaten something potentially dangerous, or even if you just suspect it, donât wait for clinical signs to appear. By then, it may already be too late. Far better to pay for an overcautious detox than risk the life of a four-legged family member.

Thanksgiving can be enjoyable for the whole family, dogs included, as long as ingredients and leftovers arenât left out for a dog to gobble down. Be familiar with ingredients that are harmful to pets, particularly anything toxic. A little care with what gets shared keeps the day safe and lets everyone relax.

#7874. Your Compost Pile Needs These 6 Things Before Winter If You Want to Make Black Gold Through the Cold

Frosty nights don't have to signal the end of the composting season. A few simple changes now can help your pile keep working through winter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Did you know that your compost pile keeps working over winter? While the decomposition process might slow, microorganisms are still active in compost as long as it doesn’t freeze. Ignoring your compost over winter is a missed opportunity to keep making and using the garden's black gold.

During winter composting, microorganisms slow down their activities, and freezing temperatures can temporarily stop them, but they won’t necessarily die. A sufficiently large and well-managed compost pile can stay warm enough in the center to keep the little critters working and breaking down waste materials.

Tackle these six tasks now to keep composting at home this winter. Even if decomposition slows in the cold, these steps will help you get more usable compost earlier next spring. Our tips work for all main types of composting, including open heaps, compost bins, and enclosed tumblers.

Now is a good time to remove any finished compost to use as winter mulch in your garden beds. Then, it’s time for one last turn for the season. Turning compost helps aerate the pile, introducing oxygen to the microorganisms that need it to decompose materials. It also distributes moisture and materials more evenly.

A sturdy garden fork will do the job, but a compost aerator tool, like this Squeeze Master one from Amazon, makes it much easier to get air deep into the pile without having to dig everything out and turn it by hand.

This should be your final turn before freezing conditions begin. You don’t want to keep turning compost over the winter, as this will release heat and slow the decomposition process. As you make the final turn, look for and break up any wet clumps or large pieces of material that haven’t broken down much. If you note a sour or rotten smell, add more dry, brown materials.

Larger compost piles retain heat better than smaller piles because they have a greater volume of material relative to their surface area, which is exposed to the cold. The more you can add to your pile now, the more likely it is that the center will remain warm and active throughout winter. A long-probe compost thermometer, like the Vivosun Compost, is a handy way to check what's happening deep inside the pile without disturbing it.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

For a compost pile, aim for three feet (0.9 m) wide, deep, and high. Bulk up your pile during your final turn, adding a good mix of green and brown materials. Be sure to add enough dry, coarse material to absorb moisture. A large pile won’t be any good if it becomes waterlogged and so compacted that there is no airflow.

While you don’t want to turn your compost again this winter, you can still add layers of waste to it as the season progresses. Green materials, like kitchen scraps, keep coming all winter, but brown materials tend to be harder to come by. Browns include dry leaves and twigs as well as cardboard, untreated paper, and straw.

Good compost should have layers of each type of material, so stockpile your harder-to-find browns now. As you add kitchen scraps over the winter, layer in some of these stockpiled brown materials to maintain a good balance. A countertop compost caddy, like the Oxo Good Grips Easy-Clean Compost Bin, makes it easy to collect kitchen waste indoors until you're ready to take it outside. Keep a bin or pile of leaves and twigs from fall yard waste, as well as shredded paper and cardboard.

A large pile with extra waste material will help insulate the active center of your compost pile, but you can also take extra steps to insulate and protect it from cold winter temperatures. This will slow heat loss. It’s important that you take insulating steps before the compost pile freezes.

One easy way to insulate the pile is to surround it on all sides with straw bales or bags of leaves. If you don't have straw on hand, you can pick up full-sized straw bales from Tractor Supply to create a protective barrier around your compost pile. You can also add a layer of straw or leaves on top. Wood chips and finished compost are also efficient insulators.

If you have a bin or tumbler, another option is to surround it with insulating materials. Just be sure you still have easy access to add materials throughout winter.

Winter precipitation can saturate a compost pile, causing it to become compacted and reducing airflow. Moisture can also wash away the valuable nutrients you’re trying to collect. If you have an open compost pile, cover it with a tarp that will allow precipitation to run off and away from the compost. A heavy-duty Everbilt tarp from Home Depot is a durable option that you can secure in place to keep winter rain and snow out. If you have a bin, keep a lid on it.

While keeping moisture out is important, compost still needs airflow in winter. Don’t completely seal your pile with protective coverings. If you have a bin with a cover, there should be drainage and air holes. Make sure these don’t get clogged.

Moisture balance is always important in compost. It’s important to check and adjust this balance before your compost freezes this winter. To optimize microorganism activity, the composting material should feel damp when you squeeze it in your hand without excess moisture running out of it.

If your compost feels too wet, incorporate more dry, brown material. If the pile is too dry, you can add a little water before there is a real danger of it freezing. Throughout winter, as long as temperatures allow it, continue to check the pile for moisture balance and adjust as needed.

Many gardeners might wonder: are these efforts worthwhile, or does compost just shut down for winter? Compost does continue to break down in winter, sometimes with temporary stops during freezing conditions.

However, it’s important to have realistic expectations. While microorganisms continue to break down compostable materials in winter, their processes do slow down significantly. Larger, insulated piles are more likely to stay active and break down faster than smaller piles or compost in uninsulated bins. Taking these steps to keep your pile warmer in winter is worth the effort if you can keep microorganisms active and working.

It’s important to note that if you practice vermicomposting, you should provide extra protection for the worms over winter. To keep it active over winter, keep your vermicompost bin indoors where you can control the temperature.

Winter doesn't have to put composting on hold. A little preparation in autumn can protect valuable organic material, reduce household waste, and give you a head start on producing nutrient-rich compost for the next growing season.

These festive houseplants bring color, fragrance and greenery to your home long after the decorations come down...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A Christmas tree might be the star of the living room in December, but once the holidays are over, it usually gets packed away or recycled. Festive houseplants, on the other hand? Well, they can stick around for years – and some might become so beloved that you can't imagine your home without them.

Whether you're looking to make your Christmas décor a little more lasting, or simply a self-confessed crazy plant lady in need of more houseplants (I'm right there with you!), then you should absolutely consider choosing a living plant this year.

From spectacular seasonal blooms to fragrant herbs and miniature trees, these five festive favorites offer plenty of reasons to keep growing long after the last present has been unwrapped.

I'm a huge fan of Christmas cactus, having inherited one that lived for an incredible 27 years before recently dying. (RIP, Noel; we barely knew ye!) It was a reminder of just how long these festive houseplants can last, and how attached we can become to them over time.

Christmas cactus (Schlumbergera) produces beautiful flowers in shades of pink, red, purple and white, usually just in time for the holidays. Even when it's not in bloom, though, its arching stems make an attractive display, particularly in a hanging pot.

Give it bright indirect light, keep it away from harsh sunshine and don't let its roots sit in soggy compost (mine loved life on our bathroom windowsill), and remember: a cooler spell and shorter days in fall help encourage flowering.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Few festive houseplants make quite as dramatic a statement as amaryllis (Hippeastrum). Its tall stems and oversized trumpet-shaped flowers bring a splash of color indoors when much of the garden is dormant, making it a favorite for Christmas displays.

Somehow, I have managed to keep my own diva alive for several years now (it's sitting on my desk as I type this, in fact), so I urge you not to discard the bulb once flowering finishes. Instead, remove the faded flowers, keep the leaves growing, give it light, water and occasional feeding as it grows, then follow a suitable resting period to encourage another round of blooms. With a little patience, the same bulb can reward you with flowers for many seasons.

You can pick up a bag of Amaryllis bulbs easily enough from the Garden State Bulb Store, if you fancy giving it a go; they'd make excellent holiday presents once you've gotten them started!

If you'd prefer something compact and relatively easy to care for, Flaming Katy (Kalanchoe blossfeldiana) is a solid choice. This succulent produces clusters of bright flowers in red, pink, orange, yellow or white, and it's widely available during the festive season.

Its fleshy leaves store water, so it doesn't need constant watering (making it ideal for even the most forgetful plant parents everywhere). All you have to do is place it somewhere bright, allow the compost to dry a little between drinks, and avoid leaving it sitting in water.

Blooming in the fall and winter, what could be prettier than this Flaming Katy at Christmas?

Flaming Katy can be encouraged to flower again by providing a steady stint of uninterrupted nights in autumn, making it a holiday plant that's well worth keeping after its first colorful display.

Rosemary is a lovely way to bring fragrance into the home over the holidays, especially when sold clipped into a miniature living Christmas tree shape. Its evergreen needles look festive, while its scent adds a little something extra to the season – and you can snip sprigs for cooking, too.

I have actually kept my own rosemary going for a long time, bringing it in and out of the house with the seasons until it grew so large that it eventually had to move permanently into the garden. It just goes to show that a small festive plant can have quite a future ahead of it!

Rosemary (even one like this Rosemary Christmas Tree from the Three Company Store) needs plenty of light and well-drained compost. Don't overwater it, and remember that it generally prefers cooler and brighter conditions than a hot room right next to a radiator.

For something a little different, why not choose a small tree? Fig, olive and citrus trees can all make beautiful container plants, bringing Mediterranean charm to a bright home.

A fig tree offers attractive foliage and the possibility of homegrown fruit, while an olive tree has silvery-green leaves and a timeless look. And there's no denying that a calamondin or miniature orange tree is particularly festive, with glossy foliage, fragrant flowers and colorful fruit that can linger on the branches.

Naturally, these trees need the brightest spot you can offer, and citrus in particular appreciates warmth and consistent care. Indoor conditions aren't always ideal year-round, so check each tree's needs and consider moving it outdoors during suitable warmer months.

A living Christmas plant is a gift that doesn't have to end when the festivities do. Choose yourself, then, a festive houseplant that suits your space, give it the care it needs, and you could be enjoying your festive favorite for many Christmases to come.

Or, you know, you could ask Santa to bring you one. Either or...

Old-style holiday bulbs that run hot can help reduce the chill for potted plants on a frosty night. But there are a few details to get right before you try it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Every November, boxes of holiday lights come down from the attic, and a few gardeners start eyeing those tangled strands for a second job. On paper, Christmas lights frost protection sounds like a neighbor's tip over coffee – string up a potted lemon tree, plug it in, and hope it makes it to morning.

There's some truth to it. Gardeners have relied on heat from old-style bulbs for years, and it can work alongside the usual steps for winterizing container plants, like covering pots or moving them under shelter. When used safely with a suitable cover or enclosure, that heat can nudge the temperature around a plant up a few degrees.

The catch is that only certain bulbs produce enough heat to help, and most modern porch strands won't help at all. But using the right bulbs comes with its own risks. Mix hot bulbs, fabric covers, and unprotected electrical connections outdoors carelessly, and you have a fire and shock hazard.

Christmas lights keep plants warm only if the bulbs run hot. Old-fashioned incandescent bulbs, like these C7 Christmas lights from Amazon, give off a fair amount of heat along with their light, so running a strand beneath a properly supported frost cover or inside a cold frame can warm the small area around a plant. University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources advises home citrus growers to use traditional non-LED lights to provide extra warmth, with or without a frost blanket.

Colorado State University Extension measured the effect in cold frame trials in Fort Collins. One string of 25 mid-size C7 bulbs hung inside a covered cold frame, with a space blanket over the frame, kept each frame noticeably warmer than the night outside. A string also beat a single large bulb at warming the cold corners.

If you want to recreate an enclosed space like that, use a cold frame or mini greenhouse, but only if the structure allows the lights to be safely suspended away from the plants and covering.

Pick up a string of Christmas lights in a store today, and you'll likely find they're LEDs. They convert far more of their electricity into light, leaving little heat behind – fine for decoration but useless for shielding a citrus tree on a 28°F (-2°C) night. When it comes to LED lights, frost protection just isn't on the table – they don't generate enough warmth.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

University frost guidelines specifically recommend incandescent bulbs when you need real heat. Traditional incandescent mini lights can provide some warmth, while larger C7 and C9 bulbs, like these from Novelty Lights Store, produce more heat per bulb.

Any set used should carry an outdoor rating and be suitable for the intended setup. With incandescent Christmas lights, plants under a properly supported cover can gain extra heat, but the same heat makes the bulbs a hazard if they touch foliage or covering materials.

Several vulnerable container plants could benefit, but growers most often protect potted citrus this way. Cold damage can begin around 30°F (-1°C), depending on the variety and duration of exposure, with limes generally more sensitive than mandarins. A potted lemon on the patio faces a specific risk that an in-ground tree doesn't. Its roots are far less cold-hardy than its branches, and the small amount of potting mix around them can cool and freeze much faster than the soil around an in-ground tree.

That means the lights can help through brief cold spells – just a few nights with light frost. They're not enough to protect tropical plants during weeks of hard freezes. A larger container holds more potting mix and can provide some extra insulation for the roots, so a pot like the ModernNest fiberstone planter from Walmart, designed to withstand freezing conditions, gives a citrus tree a sturdier home but won't prevent its roots from freezing.

Hot incandescent bulbs can cause damage if they come into contact with foliage or covering materials. Incandescent bulbs can burn leaves if they touch them directly. Frost cloth, sheets, plastic wrap, and space blankets should never be pressed against the lights, where they can scorch, melt, or become a fire risk. Hang the strand so each bulb has enough clearance from surrounding materials, and use a separate frame, stakes, or supports to keep covers up and away from the bulbs. Make sure the lights are securely positioned so they cannot shift into contact with the covering.

Water and electricity can create hazards on cold nights. Use only outdoor-rated lights and cords outside, and plug them into a GFCI-protected outlet. Throw out any strand with cracked sockets or frayed wire instead of hanging it. Keep indoor strands and household power strips indoors, and don't rely on tape to waterproof electrical connections. Follow the manufacturer's limits on how many strings can be connected end to end, and follow the safety instructions packed with the product.

Start by moving the pot. An unheated garage, shed, or closed-in porch that stays above freezing can carry a citrus tree through a cold snap with no wiring. Pots that stay outside belong together, up against a house wall or in a corner out of the wind. Water them well before the cold comes, since moist potting mix freezes more slowly than dry.

Covers and wraps add another layer. Lowe's sells a 2-ounce frost blanket that can go over the plant on cold nights and come off during the day. Around the container, slip on an Eonox drawstring pot insulation cover to keep cold wind off the root zone.

For plants that need steady heat for weeks, a thermostatically controlled heater inside a greenhouse built to house one is the safer setup – the Dr Infrared greenhouse heater has an adjustable thermostat.

Under a cover or in a cold frame, old incandescent holiday lights can add a few degrees, maybe enough to see potted citrus through a short, light frost. You can't count on them, though, and the method needs careful setup, even though it's recommended by several university extension services. An LED strand won't give a cold plant any real protection.

Using hot bulbs with fabric and outdoor power for improvised heating carries risks that are easy to underestimate. Proper shelter, insulation, and a good frost blanket are generally safer options, although they won't always provide as much warmth as a safely heated enclosure.

For most gardeners, the simplest solution is to keep the twinkling lights on the porch this year and move your lemon tree into a frost-free garage when cold weather hits. It'll still be green when the holiday decorations go back in the attic.

#7867. No Pseudonymity for Man Suing Trump+Rubio+Musk over Ukraine-Related Actions

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Chief Judge James Boasberg (D.C.C.) today in Doe v. Trump:

Plaintiff Michael Doe is an American citizen whose wife and daughter reside in Kyiv, Ukraine. In March 2025, his wife and daughter were almost killed in a drone strike. On behalf of himself and a class of Ukrainian refugees, Doe sues President Trump, Secretary Rubio, and Elon Musk for violating, inter alia, a federal statute that imposes sanctions on Russia, the Take Care Clause, and the First Amendment. [The claims are apparently related to the Trump Administration's actions related to sanctions on Russia Musk's actions related to Ukraine and Starlink. -EV]

Generally, a complaint must identify the plaintiffs. That requirement reflects the "presumption in favor of disclosure [of litigants' identities], which stems from the 'general public interest in the openness of governmental processes,' and, more specifically, from the tradition of open judicial proceedings." A party moving to proceed pseudonymously thus "bears the weighty burden of both demonstrating a concrete need for such secrecy[] and identifying the consequences that would likely befall it if forced to proceed in its own name." …

Plaintiff has not established that his interest in pseudonymity outweighs the public's interest in learning his identity….

The Court does not doubt that individuals in Kyiv face brutal, life-threatening dangers, nor does it take their—or their families'—concerns about safety lightly. Plaintiff has failed, however, to link those legitimate fears to his being publicly named in this lawsuit. He provides no evidence that Russia's extensive bombing campaign targets the family members of individuals engaged in Russian-sanction-related lawsuits in the United States. At most, he asserts that "[t]he Russian government have a proven documented history and pattern of targeting anyone, anywhere in the world, who challenges their authority of government," including "documented attempted assassinations" and "the use of sophisticated hacking groups to steal identities, digital assets[,] and to launch drone bombing attacks inside Ukraine."

Doe's broad assertion that Russian retaliates against critics does not establish that it will assassinate him, steal his identity or digital assets, or launch drone strikes at his family members in Ukraine in response to a lawsuit. Absent any specific threats or evidence that his family members will be so targeted, this factor weighs against pseudonymity….

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Work out why your Christmas cactus hasn't got buds yet, and discover what you can still fix in November.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A Christmas cactus not blooming is a common holiday letdown, and it stings more when the plant seems perfectly healthy with plump green stems. And you ask yourself, why won't my Christmas cactus flower when the plant looks just fine? A Christmas cactus not showing buds by the end of November is usually reacting to light, warmth, water or a move at the wrong moment. And, once you've worked out what the cause is, there's still time to fix some mistakes so you can enjoy the holiday flower show.

A healthy Christmas cactus doesn't automatically mean you have a holiday houseplant that's ready to flower. Buds form in response to fall conditions – long dark nights and cooler temperatures – and many folk create the exact environment to make sure a Christmas cactus blooms right on time for the holidays. So, unless it gets those triggers to start forming buds, the plant won't flower even if you give your Christmas cactus all the care it needs in November to keep it healthy. Another common problem with a Christmas cactus not flowering is that it does form buds, but drops them before they open.

There are five common mistakes that lead to zero holiday flowers. Which of these issues is the reason why your Christmas cactus doesn't have buds yet?

Holiday cacti set flower buds when nights grow long. They need about 13 to 14 hours of uninterrupted darkness each night for six weeks or more, and that dark period must be truly dark. Even a table lamp switched on in the evening, a street light shining through the window or a hallway light left on overnight can interrupt the cycle, causing the plant to keep making stems instead of buds. This mistake shows up as no buds at all.

If you suspect this is the reason your Schlumbergera doesn't have buds yet, place your plant in complete darkness after dinner then bring it back to bright, indirect light in the morning. A dark room that isn't used is perfect, and you can block any artificial light coming through the window with blackout curtains like Sun Zero Curtain Panels, available from Walmart. Another option is simply to cover the plant in an upturned cardboard box overnight.

Once buds have set, night length stops mattering as much, so evening light isn't a problem.

Cool nights are the other half of the trigger to get a Christmas cactus to flower. Holiday cacti need nights between 50°F and 59°F (10–15°C) to set buds, so keep a living room warm all evening with the furnace running and that signal disappears.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Move your Christmas cactus to a cooler spot at night, not a cold one. An unheated bedroom or a sunroom that cools down after dark often works, as long as temperature doesn't dip below 50°F (10°C). It's hard to guess how cool a room gets at three o'clock in the morning so a cheap indoor thermometer that records the maximum and minimum temperatures, like the TempPro digital indoor thermometer on Amazon, is handy to check the overnight number.

Once your plant has formed buds, it'' still very sensitive to environmental conditions, so be sure to avoid the common spots that cause a Christmas cactus to lose its buds.

Holiday cacti aren't desert cacti. They grow on rainforest trees in Brazil so don't like to bake dry the way a barrel cactus loves. Let the potting mix dry out hard while buds are forming and the plant may make fewer of them, or wilt and drop the ones it has. Keep the mix soggy and the roots can rot, which ends the same way – limp stems and buds on the floor.

Once buds appear, keep the potting mix evenly moist but never wet. An easy way to check if your Christmas cactus needs watering is to push a long wooden skewer like these bamboo skewers from Walmart to the bottom of the pot and pull it out: if damp soil clings to the wood, wait a few days before watering again. An indoor watering can with a long goose-neck spout like this houseplant can from Walmart makes it much easier to be precise about how much water you're giving your plant. Empty the saucer after every watering too.

Once buds have formed, moving your plant is one of the easiest ways to lose them. Any sudden shift in light, temperature or humidity can trigger bud loss. Christmas cacti are so sensitive to their environment, it's not just moving the plant from a cool back bedroom to a warm, dim spot beside the tree that causes bud drop. Even moving your holiday houseplant to a different spot in the same room or rotating the pot can be enough to lose those precious buds.

Choose the spot where your plant will stay through the holidays as soon as buds appear, then leave it there. Check that spot for heat and drafts first. Buds also drop on plants near heating vents, a gas fireplace or a bowl of ripening fruit which gives off ethylene gas. The same care applies if you buy a plant with buds already set, such as this pack of 2 Holiday Christmas Cactus from Costa Farms, via The Home Depot. Ask for the plant to be wrapped against the cold for the trip home and put it in its final spot as soon as it arrives. A few buds will fall while it settles in but most will stay put as long as you don't move the plant again.

Holiday cacti should only be fed during active growth from spring through late summer, so don't fertilize after September. That break from fertilizer helps plants set more flower buds in fall. November feeding won't help a plant that already lacks buds and, on a stressed plant, extra salts in the pot do more harm than good.

Wait until the flowers finish and new growth starts in spring, then use a balanced food for indoor flowering plants such as Espoma Organic Violet! plant food, available on Amazon, once a month at half strength through summer.

If you don't see any signs of buds on your holiday houseplant by late November, it's worth trying the banana bag trick to trigger Christmas cactus blooms. However, flowers will likely open in early January rather than on Christmas morning.

Next year, start the dark nights in late September or early October so the timing lines up. Buds usually show up three to four weeks after long nights begin, and the flowers open after roughly six to eight weeks of short days.

A plant that already has small buds at its stem tips in mid-November has done the hard part, however, so as long as you keep your Christmas cactus in one spot that's not too warm at night, and evenly moist, those flowers should open on schedule.

#7860. Gun Rights and Guilt by Association

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Some excerpts from the longish opinion today in Shilling v. County of San Diego, decided today by Ninth Circuit Judge Patrick Bumatay, joined by Judges Kenneth Lee and Jennifer Sung:

The San Diego County Sheriff revoked Kenneth Shilling's concealed-carry weapon ("CCW") license over his affiliation with the Boozefighters Motorcycle Club…. [We conclude, among other things, that] the district court improperly dismissed his First Amendment [freedom of association] claim….

Kenneth Charles Shilling resides in San Diego, California. He's a member of the Boozefighters Motorcycle Club, which, according to Shilling, was founded in 1946 by World War II veterans. In his view, it's not like some other motorcycle clubs, which are known for criminal and gang activity. Instead, the Boozefighters focus on charitable work and the "core values of family, work, and community." Shilling's record is clean; he has no criminal history.

In June 2022, when the "good moral character" requirement [for getting a concealed carry license] still existed [under California law], Shilling applied for and received a CCW license from then-San Diego County Sheriff Anthony Ray. This was short lived. Less than a year and a half later, in December 2023, a different San Diego County Sheriff, Kelly Martinez, used the "good moral character" requirement to revoke Shilling's CCW license. In a letter notifying Shilling of the revocation, Sheriff Martinez explained that the "San Diego Sheriff's Department['s] good moral character definition" excludes a person who:

Has a pattern of or propensity for criminal conduct, as demonstrated by anything in the application or investigation for a license. This includes, but is not limited to, evidence of criminal behavior or a close nexus to a criminal gang. In making this determination, the Sheriff's Department shall use an objective inquiry, considering the facts and circumstances known at the time of the application or through the investigation.

The letter said that Shilling's license was revoked due to his association with the Boozefighters Motorcycle Club, which the Sheriff described as a "criminal street gang." Shilling was not given the opportunity to contest the allegations before his license was revoked, but he could request reconsideration of the decision. The new CCW regime with the "dangerousness" requirement took effect on January 1, 2024, shortly after Shilling's license was revoked….

Here's the court's analysis allowing Shilling's First Amendment freedom of association claim to go forward:

The First Amendment guarantees all Americans the "right to associate with others." … [T]he right protects groups of individuals "in pursuit of a wide variety of political, social, economic, educational, religious and cultural ends." …

The government may infringe the freedom of association in "varied ways," including by "punish[ing] individuals for their affiliations." The government cannot impose "criminal sanctions or deny[ ] rights and privileges solely because of a citizen's association with an unpopular organization." For example, a group of students could not be denied the "benefits" of official campus recognition at a state college merely because of its affiliation with a national organization associated with disruptive and violent campus activity…. [Likewise,] "Civil liability may not be imposed merely because an individual belonged to a group, some members of which committed acts of violence." … If the government seeks to deprive an individual of a benefit, privilege, or right based on association with an alleged criminal organization, "it is necessary to establish that the group itself possessed unlawful goals and that the individual held a specific intent to further those illegal aims." …

Given this understanding of the First Amendment, Shilling easily pleaded a violation of his freedom of association…. [His] allegations sufficiently raise an infringement of Shilling's free-association right because the Sheriff deprived him of a benefit, privilege, or right—the ability to carry a concealed weapon in public—"solely because of [his] association with an unpopular organization." Unless the Sheriff adequately meets her burden of showing the Boozefighters "possessed unlawful goals" and Shilling's "specific intent to further those illegal aims," she cannot "punish [Shilling] for [his] affiliations." This kind of "guilt by association alone, without establishing that an individual's association poses the threat feared by the Government, is an impermissible basis upon which to deny First Amendment rights."

In dismissing this claim, the district court misunderstood the nature of the free-association right. It asserted that Shilling had to show the revocation of his CCW license somehow prevented him from associating with the Boozefighters Motorcycle Club or participating in the Club's activities. While preventing an individual from participating in a group's lawful activities may be one way to violate the First Amendment right, it's infringed in "varied ways." And "denying" an individual benefits, rights, or privileges "solely because of [his] association"—as Shilling alleges—is certainly another way….

For the court's analysis of sovereign immunity and of whether Schilling's Second Amendment claim was moot, see the full opinion.

Gary W. Gorski (Veterans Law Center) represents plaintiff.

You don't need to splash out on a premium tree this Christmas. With a little know-how, you can turn a budget option into something truly special.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When you take the kids out to choose a Christmas tree, everyone has in mind a lush, deep green, perfectly shaped evergreen that is featured in holiday advertisements. But not every evergreen in the lot has that kind of sex appeal, especially budget trees for sale in grocery stores, supermarkets, and big-box retailers. These affordable trees can look thin, sparse, and like they didn’t get any sleep last night.

But don’t worry, an inexpensive grocery store Christmas tree can be “spruced up” nicely with a few simple tricks. Yes, you can turn ugly ducklings into beautiful centerpieces by taking steps to make a Christmas tree look fuller, well-structured, and fresh. I’ll explain how to make a real Christmas tree look better with Christmas tree care tips that boost your tree's wow-power.

In this guide, I'm going to walk you through the easy steps you can take to improve your tree dramatically, from a sparse Christmas tree to a festive showstopper. And I promise it won’t cost you a fortune.

There are many reasons that a freshly cut Christmas tree can look droopy and sparse in the store. These include transport stress and dehydration. One of the quickest fixes with a big punch is to make a fresh cut on the bottom of the trunk, taking off around ½ inch. A good folding saw, such as the Rexberi 11-Inch Folding Saw from Amazon, will make light work of this, and it's handy for pruning jobs around the garden, too.

Immediately after cutting, pop the tree into a sturdy stand with water. The Krinner Genie Christmas Tree Stand has a foot-pedal mechanism that makes it easy to secure the tree, plus a built-in water reservoir. But it's not cheap, and if you're buying a budget tree, chances are you'll want a budget-friendly stand to go with it. The Leejec Christmas Tree Stand is a good, affordable alternative, with a generous water reservoir and a handy water level indicator.

Don't leave the tree sitting around after making the cut. The cut surface can dry out, reducing moisture uptake, so getting it into water promptly gives it the best chance of staying fresh.

That sorrowful evergreen you brought home needs time to relax. Once you prune off the very bottom of the trunk, set the tree in a bucket of water and give it time to rehydrate. Leave it wrapped in its netting overnight, which will also make it easier to maneuver into its stand the next day.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Once the tree is securely in place, remove the wrapping and let the branches gradually drop and spread into their natural shape for a few hours. You might be surprised how much fuller it looks after a little time to settle.

Now it's time to give your tree a little makeover. Walk around it and look carefully at its shape. There will likely be a few stray or uneven branches that need tidying up, particularly if you've bought a cheaper tree that hasn't been professionally shaped.

To prune your Christmas tree, take a sharp pair of bypass pruners – Fiskars Bypass Pruning Shears from Amazon are a good, affordable option – and start by removing any broken, damaged, or awkwardly protruding branches. Trim back overly long branches to a side shoot where possible, rather than cutting bluntly through the tips.

Pay particular attention to the lower branches. Remove any that drag on the floor or interfere with the stand, making clean cuts close to the trunk without damaging the bark. This will give the tree a neater silhouette and make it easier to reach the water reservoir.

Step back regularly to check your progress, working toward a balanced cone shape without making the tree look unnaturally perfect. Go easy, though – you can always take more off, but you can't put a branch back.

Starting at the bottom of the tree, gently separate any branches that have become compressed during transport. Work your way upward, easing crowded branches apart and encouraging them to spread into their natural positions. Take care not to force stiff branches, as they can snap.

Once you've worked your way around the tree, step back and look for any obvious gaps. You may be able to gently reposition flexible branches to make the tree look fuller, but avoid bending or twisting them into unnatural shapes.

Pay particular attention to the lower branches, spreading them outward where possible to help disguise the trunk and tree stand. Near the top, gently separate crowded branches to create a more balanced, tapered shape. Don't worry about making everything perfectly symmetrical – a little natural irregularity is part of the charm of a real Christmas tree.

Have you ever used hair extensions? Or had a friend who used hair weaving to change the volume of their hair? You can use this same technique to fill in the canopy of your Christmas tree by tucking extra evergreen branches into bare spots. It’s a quick way to give a sparse Christmas tree a fuller figure.

What to use for this type of branch extension? Start with any healthy branches you removed when pruning your tree earlier. You can also use evergreen clippings from your own yard or ask for spare branches from the Christmas tree lot. Choose branches that closely match your tree for the most natural finish, or mix two or three types of evergreen to add depth and texture.

For larger bare patches, try tucking in realistic faux evergreen sprays, like these Hananona pine branches. Cedar and pine sprays work particularly well, blending into the natural foliage while adding extra volume.

Tuck the cut ends in toward the trunk, positioning the foliage to disguise any obvious gaps. Use green floral wire, like this Pauleen wire from Amazon, to secure the stems discreetly to existing branches, making sure they're firmly attached. Step back occasionally to check the overall effect, adding a few more sprigs wherever the tree still looks sparse.

We all have good sides and bad sides, and your Christmas tree might too. If one side is lopsided or less impressive, simply turn it toward the wall. Of course, this trick works less well if you have a revolving tree stand.

Some gaps may still be visible after fluffing up the branches and adding extras, but that's where clever decorating comes to the rescue. Tuck large ornaments deep inside the tree, closer to the trunk, to disguise bare spots and create a sense of depth.

Another great trick is to cluster smaller ornaments in groups of three to make sparse areas look fuller. If one part of the tree is overloaded with decorations, move a few into the gaps to create a more balanced look. You can also use pinecones, artificial flowers, or decorative picks to add texture and interest.

Finally, try weaving wide ribbons or garlands through the branches to disguise any remaining gaps. Rather than wrapping them tightly around the outside, tuck sections deeper into the tree and let them billow outward. This creates the illusion of a much fuller, more luxurious Christmas tree without spending a fortune.

Keeping your tree looking good until Christmas requires a little effort. Here are some top tips:
